docs.title: inference4j
docs.text:
Run AI models in Java. Three lines of code, zero setup.

inference4j is an inference-only AI library for Java built on ONNX Runtime. It provides ergonomic, type-safe APIs for running model inference locally — no API keys, no network calls, no third-party services. Pass a String, BufferedImage, or Path, get Java objects back.

docs.title: What can you do with inference4j?
docs.text: Want to see it in action? Check out inference4j-showcase — a local demo app you can run to explore every capability the library provides.

docs.title: Sentiment Analysis
docs.text:
try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder().build()) {
    System.out.println(classifier.classify("This movie was fantastic!"));
    // [TextClassification[label=POSITIVE, confidence=0.9998]]
}

docs.text:
try (var classifier = DebertaZeroShotClassifier.builder().build()) {
    List<TextClassification> result = classifier.classify(
        "My invoice shows the same charge twice.",
        List.of("billing", "outage", "feature request", "account access"));
    // billing 0.97, account access 0.02, ...
}

docs.title: What you don't have to do
docs.text:
• No tokenization — WordPiece tokenizers are built in and handled automatically
  • No tensor handling — pass a String, BufferedImage, or Path; get Java objects back
  • No ONNX session setup — builder().build() handles everything
  • No model downloads — auto-downloaded from HuggingFace and cached on first use
  • No Python sidecar — pure Java, runs anywhere Java runs

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Running a trained ML model in Java sounds simple — load the model, pass some data, get a result. In practice, the inference call itself is the easy part. The hard part is everything around it: preprocessing and postprocessing.

Before a model can process an image, someone has to resize it, normalize the pixel values, rearrange the channels into the right layout (NCHW? NHWC?), and pack the result into a multi-dimensional float array called a tensor. After the model runs, someone has to interpret the raw output tensor — apply softmax to get probabilities, decode token IDs back into text, map class indices to human-readable labels, run non-maximum suppression to filter overlapping bounding boxes.

This work requires understanding the model's internals: its expected input shape, normalization constants, output format, and decoding strategy. ML engineers deal with this routinely. Java developers who need to ship a model to production shouldn't have to.

docs.title: Built on ONNX
docs.text: inference4j embraces ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) as its runtime platform. ONNX is an open standard for representing ML models — a model trained in PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX can be exported to a single .onnx file and run anywhere via ONNX Runtime. This means inference4j can run models from any training framework without depending on that framework at runtime. No Python, no TensorFlow, no PyTorch — just a .onnx file and the ONNX Runtime native library.

docs.title: What inference4j does
docs.text:
The vast majority of inference tasks follow the same three-stage pattern: preprocess → infer → postprocess. inference4j provides curated wrappers that handle all three stages, so you work with standard Java types instead of tensors:

%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '18px'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    Input["<b>Java Object</b><br>String, BufferedImage, Path"]

    subgraph inference4j["inference4j wrapper"]
        Pre["<b>Preprocess</b><br>tokenize text, resize/normalize image, load audio"]
        Infer["<b>Infer</b><br>ONNX Runtime forward pass"]
        Post["<b>Postprocess</b><br>softmax, decode, NMS, label mapping"]
        Pre --> Infer --> Post
    end

    Output["<b>Java Object</b><br>Classification, Transcription, Detection"]

    Input --> Pre
    Post --> Output

Each wrapper encapsulates the model-specific knowledge — the normalization constants, the tokenizer, the output decoding — so you don't have to.

docs.title: Where it fits
docs.text:
Java has great tools for building AI-powered applications. Spring AI provides an excellent abstraction layer for LLM orchestration. DJL offers engine-agnostic model training and inference. LangChain4j simplifies LLM-powered workflows.

inference4j doesn't compete with any of them. It fills a different gap: taking a specific ONNX model and making it trivial to call from Java, with all the preprocessing and postprocessing handled for you.

  • 3-line integration for popular models — builder().build(), call a method, get Java objects back
  • Standard Java types in, standard Java types out — no tensor abstractions leak into your code
  • Inference only — optimized for production serving, not training
  • Lightweight — each wrapper is a thin layer over ONNX Runtime, not a framework
  • Complements the ecosystem — use inference4j to run your embedding model, Spring AI to orchestrate your LLM chain, both in the same application

Learn more about the pipeline architecture in How It Works.

docs.title: Using LangChain4j?
docs.text:
LangChain4j adapters

The inference4j-langchain4j module provides inference4j models as implementations of LangChain4j interfaces, running in-process:

  • PII redaction as a DocumentTransformer
  • Prompt-injection detection as an InputGuardrail
  • OCR and speech-to-text as DocumentParsers
  • Embeddings as an EmbeddingModel and reranking as a ScoringModel

See inference4j for LangChain4j and RAG pipelines.

docs.title: v0.10.0 — NER & Embeddings
docs.text:

  • [x] NamedEntityRecognizer interface, NamedEntity result type (entity text, label, character offsets, confidence)

docs.title: v0.10.1 — Dependency refresh
docs.text:
• [x] onnxruntime-genai 0.12.0 → 0.15.2 — refreshed our shadow build; picks up upstream security fixes and Gemma 4 / int8 support
  • [x] ONNX Runtime 1.23.0 → 1.26.0 — matches the version the genai natives are built against, so both modules load the same native library

docs.title: v0.11.0 — Spring Boot 4
docs.text:
• [x] Spring Boot 4 starter — the starter now targets Spring Boot 4.0+ / Spring Framework 7
  • [x] Actuator health types moved to org.springframework.boot.health.contributor
  • [x] Migration guide for existing users

Spring Boot 3.x left open-source support on 30 June 2026, and Spring AI 2.0 (GA June 2026) requires Boot 4 and cannot load in a 3.x context. Boot 4 is also binary-incompatible with Boot 3 for the actuator health types the starter uses, so a single artifact cannot serve both — 0.10.1 is the final Boot 3 release and remains on Maven Central, frozen.

Only the starter is affected. inference4j-core and every other module have no Spring dependency.

docs.title: v0.12.0 — Depth Estimation
docs.text:
• [x] Tensor.toFloats3D() — strict 3D reshape mirroring toFloats2D(), composing with squeeze() for batched model output
  • [x] TensorImages — dense model output to BufferedImage: grayscale, RGB from CHW planes, and colormapped rendering
  • [x] Colormap — grayscale, viridis and turbo ramps for visualizing dense output
  • [x] MathOps.minMax / minMaxNormalize — the spatial helpers dense output needs
  • [x] Depth estimation — DepthEstimator, DepthMap, and DepthAnythingEstimator (Depth Anything V2 Small)

The first four are the shared foundation for pixel-level tasks that CLAUDE.md had flagged as a prerequisite. Depth estimation is its first consumer; semantic segmentation and super-resolution are unblocked behind it.

docs.title: v0.13.0 — Long input, Whisper & readable transcripts
docs.text:
Long input, processed in full or rejected — never silently cut

  • [x] TruncationPolicy — every token-limited wrapper either truncates with a warning (default) or fails with InputTooLongException; generators use the model's real position limit instead of a fixed 512
  • [x] TokenWindows and .stride(int) — overlapping windows for NER and punctuation (lossless), the embedder (weighted average) and the reranker (MaxP)
  • [x] WindowAggregation — the text classifier combines window scores with mean(), max() or a custom lambda
  • [x] WordPieceTokenizer parity with HuggingFace — ASCII symbols split, accents stripped for uncased models, control characters dropped
  • [x] Prefill memory — generation no longer copies [prompt × vocabulary] logits into the heap

Speech

  • [x] Whisper end to end — inference4j/whisper-tiny-genai and whisper-small-genai exported with onnxruntime-genai's model builder; WhisperSpeechModel is a SpeechRecognizer
  • [x] SegmentedSpeechRecognizer — cuts long audio at voice-activity pauses; whisper-small word error rate on TED-LIUM long-form drops from 11.7% to 3.7%
  • [x] Punctuation, casing & sentence segmentation — PunctCapSegModel, plus PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer to make Wav2Vec2 transcripts readable
  • [x] SileroVadDetector.speechPadding — keeps word edges from being clipped

Platform

  • [x] ONNX Runtime 1.28.0 and onnxruntime-genai 0.17.0 — the official genai Java release, redistributed on Maven Central; one native ONNX Runtime on the classpath
  • [x] onnxruntime-genai is the default engine for LLMs, vision-language and speech
  • [x] Fixes — genai wrappers no longer repeat the last token; UnigramTokenizer maps unknown characters to unk; boolean tensors supported

docs.title: v0.13.1 — Generation fixes & newer LLMs
docs.text:
• [x] Chat prompts keep their end — over-long prompts keep the chat template and the end of the message, so the model still answers instead of continuing the text (#76)
  • [x] Qwen2.5 chat-template tokens — special tokens are read from tokenizer_config.json, so the template is no longer tokenized as plain text
  • [x] KV cache stays native — NativeTensors and InferenceSession.runNative; heap per generated token no longer grows with context (#99)
  • [x] Spring Boot auto-configuration for the genai wrappers — TextGenerator, VisionLanguageModel, WhisperSpeechModel (#90)
  • [x] Newer genai LLMs — Qwen3-0.6B, SmolLM3-3B and Phi-4-mini presets (#87)

docs.title: v0.14.0 — Zero-shot NLP, guardrails, OCR & LangChain4j
docs.text:
Zero-shot NLP, guardrails and RAG

  • [x] Zero-shot NER — GlinerEntityRecognizer: entity types given at call time, GLiNER small v2.1 and a PII-tuned model (both Apache-2.0), matching the gliner Python package; ZeroShotEntityRecognizer interface (#101)
  • [x] Prompt-injection detector — DebertaPromptInjectionDetector, a DeBERTa-v3 guardrail classifier (Apache-2.0 default; Llama Prompt Guard 2 through a user-supplied source, since it is gated). UnigramTokenizer now applies the tokenizer.json normalizer (SentencePiece Precompiled, Strip, Replace), matching HuggingFace token for token on DeBERTa-v3 and T5 (#102)
  • [x] Zero-shot text classification — DebertaZeroShotClassifier: NLI-based, labels chosen at call time, single- or multi-label; DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot v2.0 "-c" models (MIT, commercially-friendly training data), matching the HuggingFace pipeline (#103)
  • [x] Modern embeddings — nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (8K context, task prefixes) and Matryoshka .dimensions(int) on SentenceTransformerEmbedder (#104)
  • [x] LangChain4j adapter — inference4j-langchain4j: EmbeddingModel, ScoringModel, OCR and audio document parsers, PII redaction and a prompt-injection input guardrail (#111); see the LangChain4j guide (#152)
  • [x] Encoder-decoder KV cache stays native — FlanT5, BART, MarianMT, CoEdIT and T5SqlGenerator keep both caches in ONNX Runtime memory; heap per generated token drops from 2–21 MB to under 2 MB (#119)

Speech

  • [x] Moonshine v2 speech-to-text — MoonshineRecognizer (tiny, small, medium; English) with no fixed 30-second window; works with SegmentedSpeechRecognizer (#109)
  • [x] Live transcription — streaming Moonshine: feed audio as it arrives, get line-by-line text while the speaker talks (#118)

Vision & documents

  • [x] OCR recognizer and OcrPipeline — PaddleOCR PP-OCRv6 (small and tiny) line detector and CTC recognizer, composed by OcrPipeline; CraftTextDetector fits as an alternative detector (#106). TrOCR for handwriting follows (#128)
  • [x] CRAFT detects with its default thresholds — post-processing now follows the reference implementation (max text score, separate link threshold, dilation, rotated boxes), matching it region for region (#130)
  • [x] Apache-licensed detector — RtDetrDetector (DetrDetector since 0.15.0): D-FINE small (default) and nano, RT-DETRv2 ResNet-18; NMS-free, an alternative to the AGPL-3.0 Ultralytics models, matching transformers detection for detection (#107)
  • [x] Promptable segmentation — Sam2Segmenter (SAM 2.1 tiny): click or box prompts, encode once and prompt many times, with a SegmentationMask result type shared with semantic segmentation (#108)

docs.title: Generative AI via onnxruntime-genai
docs.text:
New LLM, vision-language and speech architectures come through inference4j-genai rather than being re-implemented on the native engine. The native engine stays for encoder-decoder models (T5, BART, MarianMT) and plain HuggingFace exports.

  • [ ] Qwen vision-language — a second VisionLanguageModel backed by a Qwen VL export (#88)
  • [ ] Audio-in chat — LFM2 / Phi-4-multimodal through inference4j-genai (#89)
  • [ ] License-restricted LLMs — Llama-3.2 and Gemma-3 through a user-supplied source (#110)

docs.title: Unscheduled
docs.text:
• [ ] More embedding models — Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (needs last-token pooling and a non-BERT input path) and bge-m3 (needs external-data weights); left over from #104
  • [ ] Kokoro TTS — parked: a Java English phonemizer is too much upkeep and does not carry past English (#50)
  • [ ] Video object tracking — SAM 2.1 memory modules; experiment, needs a four-module export first (#137)
  • [ ] Semantic segmentation — SegFormer; reuses the SegmentationMask type from #108
  • [ ] Super-resolution — Real-ESRGAN. Needs denormalization before TensorImages.toRgb
  • [ ] Qwen3-Reranker — decoder-token scoring needs a new OutputOperator; see #105 for the cross-encoder reranker
  • [ ] Tiktoken tokenizer — deferred. No small, ONNX-viable model currently requires it
  • [ ] CRAFT improvements — vertical text and mixed orientation
  • [ ] Stable Diffusion — feasibility study of text-to-image on ONNX Runtime
  • [ ] More ViT models — additional Vision Transformer variants

docs.title: Dropped
docs.text:
• ~~Generic Pipeline API~~ — Pipeline.builder().stage().stage().build() adds abstraction without value. Models are too different for a generic composition framework. Named pipelines (e.g., OcrPipeline) as concrete classes instead.
  • ~~Native Whisper~~ — would require mel spectrogram / FFT preprocessing in Java to duplicate what onnxruntime-genai already does natively. Whisper ships through inference4j-genai.
  • ~~Codegen plugin~~ — generates type-safe wrappers from .onnx metadata but doesn't solve preprocessing/postprocessing, which is where the real complexity lives. Handcrafted wrappers deliver more value.

docs.title: Adding a Wrapper
docs.text: This guide explains the internals of inference4j for contributors who want to add support for a new model.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
Every wrapper follows the same three-stage pattern enforced by AbstractInferenceTask:

%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '18px'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    Input["<b>I — domain input</b><br>String, BufferedImage, Path"]

    subgraph AbstractInferenceTask["AbstractInferenceTask (final run)"]
        Pre["<b>Preprocessor</b><br>domain input → Map of String, Tensor"]
        Session["<b>InferenceSession.run()</b><br>ONNX Runtime forward pass"]
        Post["<b>Postprocessor</b><br>Map of String, Tensor → domain output"]
        Pre --> Session --> Post
    end

    Output["<b>O — domain output</b><br>Classification, Transcription, Detection"]

    Input --> Pre
    Post --> Output

The run() method is final — you can't override it. Instead, you provide a Preprocessor and a Postprocessor to the constructor, and the base class wires the pipeline together.

docs.title: AbstractInferenceTask
docs.text:
public abstract class AbstractInferenceTask<I, O> implements InferenceTask<I, O> {

    protected final InferenceSession session;
    protected final Preprocessor<I, Map<String, Tensor>> preprocessor;
    protected final Postprocessor<InferenceContext<I>, O> postprocessor;

    protected AbstractInferenceTask(
            InferenceSession session,
            Preprocessor<I, Map<String, Tensor>> preprocessor,
            Postprocessor<InferenceContext<I>, O> postprocessor) {
        // ...
    }

    @Override
    public final O run(I input) {
        Map<String, Tensor> inputs = preprocessor.process(input);
        Map<String, Tensor> outputs = session.run(inputs);
        return postprocessor.process(new InferenceContext<>(input, inputs, outputs));
    }
}

Key points:

  • I is the domain input type (String, BufferedImage, Path)
  • O is the domain output type (List<Classification>, Transcription, etc.)
  • run() is final — the pipeline sequence is not negotiable
  • You wire preprocessing and postprocessing in your constructor or builder

docs.title: InferenceContext
docs.text:
public record InferenceContext<I>(
    I input,
    Map<String, Tensor> preprocessed,
    Map<String, Tensor> outputs
) {}

The postprocessor receives the full context — not just the output tensors. This is essential when postprocessing needs information from the original input (e.g., original image dimensions for rescaling bounding boxes back to pixel coordinates).

docs.title: Preprocessor and Postprocessor
docs.text:
Both are @FunctionalInterface:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Preprocessor<I, O> {
    O process(I input);
}

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Postprocessor<I, O> {
    O process(I input);
}

They support composition via andThen() and provide a static identity() factory for no-op stages.

docs.title: Vision wrappers: ImageTransformPipeline
docs.text:
For image-based models, ImageTransformPipeline handles the BufferedImage → Tensor conversion. It composes image transforms (resize, center crop, normalize) and produces a correctly shaped float tensor.

flowchart TD
    A["BufferedImage"]

    subgraph pipeline ["ImageTransformPipeline"]
        B["Resize (e.g. 224x224)"]
        C["Center crop (optional)"]
        D["Extract RGB pixels"]
        E["Normalize<br>(pixel/255 - mean) / std"]
        F["Arrange into layout<br>NCHW or NHWC"]
        B --> C --> D --> E --> F
    end

    G["Tensor — shape: 1, 3, H, W"]

    A --> B
    F --> G

docs.title: ImageNet preset
docs.text:
For models trained on ImageNet (ResNet, VGG, etc.):

ImageTransformPipeline pipeline = ImageTransformPipeline.imagenet(224);
// mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]
// NCHW layout, size 224×224

docs.title: Custom pipeline
docs.text:
For models with different normalization (EfficientNet, YOLO, etc.), use the builder:

ImageTransformPipeline pipeline = ImageTransformPipeline.builder()
    .resize(280)
    .mean(new float[]{127f/255, 127f/255, 127f/255})
    .std(new float[]{128f/255, 128f/255, 128f/255})
    .layout(ImageLayout.NHWC)
    .build();

docs.title: Auto-detection from model
docs.text:
The AbstractImageClassifier.detectPipeline() helper reads the model's input shape from the ONNX session and auto-configures the pipeline:

  • Detects input dimensions → sets resize target
  • Detects channel position → sets NCHW or NHWC layout
  • Applies the normalization constants you provide

This means adding a new image classifier often requires only specifying the correct mean/std values — the rest is auto-detected.

docs.title: Anatomy of a wrapper
docs.text: Here's the typical structure, using ResNetClassifier as a reference:

docs.title: 1. Extend the right base class
docs.text:
public class ResNetClassifier extends AbstractImageClassifier {
    // AbstractImageClassifier extends AbstractInferenceTask<BufferedImage, List<Classification>>
    // and implements ImageClassifier (which extends Classifier<BufferedImage, Classification>)
}

Choose your base:

Base class When to use AbstractInferenceTask<I, O> Any task — most flexible AbstractImageClassifier Image classification (provides classify() methods, top-K, label mapping) Direct interface implementation Stateful models (e.g., SileroVadDetector manages hidden state across frames)

docs.title: 2. Define the builder
docs.text:
Every builder offers the same three shared options, then the task's own options, then build():

try (ResNetClassifier classifier = ResNetClassifier.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/resnet50-v1-7")     // sensible default; any id the ModelSource understands
        .modelSource(new LocalModelSource(dir))   // defaults to HuggingFace
        .sessionOptions(opts -> opts.addCoreML()) // ONNX Runtime options for the model's sessions
        // ... task-specific options: labels, preprocessor, inputName, topK ...
        .build()) {
    classifier.classify(image);
}

build() validates the options, opens the model directory through the ModelSource, checks that every required file is there (failing with a ModelSourceException that names the missing file), opens the ONNX sessions, loads the companion files the options did not supply (labels, vocabulary, config), and closes everything it opened if any step fails. Start from the builder of the closest existing wrapper, such as DepthAnythingEstimator.Builder, and copy its structure: the shared loading support it extends is internal to inference4j and may change between releases.

Key conventions:

  • Default model ID — every wrapper has a sensible default pointing to the inference4j HuggingFace org
  • Public options only — the builder exposes modelId, modelSource, sessionOptions and task options; never a way to pass in an InferenceSession
  • Auto-load resources — labels, vocabulary, config are loaded from the model directory in build(), unless set on the builder
  • Tests use fixtures — tests build the wrapper from a tiny ONNX fixture in src/test/resources/fixtures through the public builder

docs.title: 3. Wire preprocessing
docs.text:
For vision, the preprocessor converts a BufferedImage into a named tensor map:

// In the constructor or builder
Preprocessor<BufferedImage, Map<String, Tensor>> preprocessor =
    image -> Map.of(inputName, imageTransformPipeline.process(image));

For NLP, tokenize text into input ID and attention mask tensors:

Preprocessor<String, Map<String, Tensor>> preprocessor = text -> {
    EncodedInput encoded = tokenizer.encode(text, maxLength);
    return Map.of(
        "input_ids", Tensor.of(encoded.inputIds()),
        "attention_mask", Tensor.of(encoded.attentionMask())
    );
};

docs.title: 4. Wire postprocessing
docs.text:
The postprocessor receives InferenceContext<I> — giving access to both the raw output tensors and the original input:

Postprocessor<InferenceContext<BufferedImage>, List<Classification>> postprocessor =
    ctx -> {
        float[] logits = ctx.outputs().get("output").toFloats();
        float[] probs = outputOperator.apply(logits);  // softmax
        int[] topIndices = MathOps.topK(probs, topK);
        return Arrays.stream(topIndices)
            .mapToObj(i -> new Classification(labels.get(i), i, probs[i]))
            .toList();
    };

docs.title: Checklist for a new wrapper
docs.text:
1. Identify the model's contract — input tensor names, shapes, normalization, output format
  2. Choose a base class — AbstractInferenceTask, AbstractImageClassifier, or direct interface implementation
  3. Implement preprocessing — convert the domain input to the tensors the model expects
  4. Implement postprocessing — convert output tensors to a meaningful Java result type
  5. Add a builder with modelId, modelSource, sessionOptions, and task-specific options
  6. Host the ONNX model under the inference4j HuggingFace org with required companion files
  7. Write tests — unit tests against a tiny ONNX fixture, integration tests with the real model
  8. Add Spring Boot auto-configuration if the wrapper should be available as a managed bean

Sharing your wrapper

If you intend to share your wrapper or model with the community, please follow the Contributing Guide for instructions on how to submit a pull request and host the model on the inference4j HuggingFace org.

docs.title: Chat Templates
docs.text: Every instruction-tuned language model expects prompts in a specific format. The model was trained on conversations structured with special marker tokens, and it will only follow instructions reliably if the prompt matches that format. A ChatTemplate tells inference4j how to wrap a user message in the correct markers before passing it to the tokenizer.

docs.title: Why models need different templates
docs.text:
During training, each model family learns to associate specific token sequences with roles in a conversation. These markers vary across model families:

Model User marker End marker Assistant marker Phi-3 <\|user\|> <\|end\|> <\|assistant\|> DeepSeek-R1 (Qwen) <\|User\|> — <\|Assistant\|> Llama / ChatML <\|im_start\|>user <\|im_end\|> <\|im_start\|>assistant

If you send a Phi-3 prompt to a DeepSeek model (or vice versa), the model won't recognize the role markers. It may ignore the instruction entirely, echo the markers back, or produce incoherent output.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
ChatTemplate is a functional interface with a single method:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface ChatTemplate {
    String format(String userMessage);
}

It takes the raw user message and returns the fully formatted prompt string. For Phi-3, the implementation looks like:

message -> "<|user|>\n" + message + "<|end|>\n<|assistant|>\n"

For a prompt like "What is Java?", this produces:

<|user|>
What is Java?<|end|>
<|assistant|>

The tokenizer then encodes this formatted string into token IDs that the model recognizes.

docs.title: onnxruntime-genai models
docs.text:
When you use ModelSources factory methods, the chat template is already configured:

// Chat template is bundled — nothing extra to configure
TextGenerator.builder()
        .model(ModelSources.phi3Mini())
        .build();

ModelSources.phi3Mini() returns a GenerativeModel that pairs the model source with the correct Phi-3 chat template. ModelSources.deepSeekR1_1_5B() does the same for DeepSeek's format.

docs.title: Native generation models
docs.text:
OnnxTextGenerator presets for instruct models (SmolLM2, Qwen2.5) come with a ChatML template preconfigured. GPT-2 is a base model (not instruction-tuned) so it has no default template, but you can provide one:

OnnxTextGenerator.gpt2()
        .chatTemplate(msg -> "Q: " + msg + "\nA:")
        .maxNewTokens(100)
        .build();

docs.title: Custom templates
docs.text:
To use a model that isn't preconfigured in ModelSources, provide both a ModelSource and a ChatTemplate:

TextGenerator.builder()
        .modelSource(myModelSource)
        .chatTemplate(msg -> "<|im_start|>user\n" + msg + "<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n")
        .build();

The template format for a given model is defined in its tokenizer_config.json file on HuggingFace, under the chat_template field. It's typically a Jinja2 template — you only need to translate the user-message portion into a Java lambda.

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text:
TextGenerator.chat(List<ChatMessage>) formats a whole conversation, with system and assistant messages, through a second method of ChatTemplate:

default String format(List<ChatMessage> messages)

The templates of the models in ModelSources implement it. A template written as a lambda formats single user messages only, and chat throws UnsupportedOperationException with it. For a custom model, implement both methods:

ChatTemplate chatMl = new ChatTemplate() {
    @Override
    public String format(String userMessage) {
        return format(List.of(ChatMessage.user(userMessage)));
    }

    @Override
    public String format(List<ChatMessage> messages) {
        StringBuilder prompt = new StringBuilder();
        for (ChatMessage message : messages) {
            prompt.append("<|im_start|>").append(message.role().name().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)).append('\n')
                    .append(message.content()).append("<|im_end|>\n");
        }
        return prompt.append("<|im_start|>assistant\n").toString();
    }
};

The LangChain4j chat model adapters use chat, so they need such a template.

docs.title: Adding support for a new model
docs.text:
When a new model family uses a chat template that isn't covered by ModelSources, you need two things:

  1. The model files — a ModelSource that resolves the ONNX weights, tokenizer, and config files
  2. The chat template — a ChatTemplate lambda that formats prompts with the correct markers

Look at the model's tokenizer_config.json for the chat_template field to find the expected format. For a simple user message (no system prompt, no tools), the relevant portion is usually a few lines of Jinja that map to a straightforward string concatenation in Java.

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text: Run autoregressive models — text generation, speech-to-text, and vision-language — directly in Java with token-by-token generation and streaming.

docs.title: Two approaches to generation
docs.text:
All models in inference4j outside this section are single-pass — one forward pass, one result. Generative models are fundamentally different. They produce output one token at a time in a loop, feeding each token back into the model to produce the next one. This loop requires managing a KV cache, token sampling, and stop conditions.

inference4j supports two approaches to running this loop:

docs.title: Native generation (inference4j-core)
docs.text:
inference4j implements the full autoregressive loop in Java on top of standard ONNX Runtime. This includes KV cache management, token sampling (temperature, top-K, top-P), BPE tokenization with decoding, and streaming — all built into inference4j-core with zero additional dependencies.

Pros:

  • Works with any ONNX model that exports KV cache inputs/outputs — the standard HuggingFace ONNX export format
  • No extra native libraries beyond ONNX Runtime
  • Full control over the generation pipeline (sampling, stop sequences, token streaming)

Cons:

  • The generation loop runs in Java rather than optimized C++, so it's slightly slower per token

docs.title: onnxruntime-genai (inference4j-genai)
docs.text:
onnxruntime-genai is a native library by Microsoft that handles the entire generation pipeline in optimized C++ — tokenization, the generation loop, KV cache, and sampling. inference4j wraps this library via the inference4j-genai module.

Pros:

  • The entire loop (including tokenization and KV cache) runs in native C++, maximizing throughput
  • Broad, fast-growing architecture coverage maintained by Microsoft — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Phi, Gemma, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, Granite, and more
  • Handles multimodal preprocessing natively — image processing for vision-language models (Phi-3.5 Vision) and audio feature extraction for speech models (Whisper)

Cons:

  • Models must be exported in onnxruntime-genai's format (a model folder with genai_config.json), either prebuilt or produced with its model builder
  • The Java API is still in preview and may change between releases
  • Requires a second native library (onnxruntime-genai), which we redistribute on Maven Central from Microsoft's official Java release
  • No encoder-decoder text models — T5, BART and MarianMT run on the native engine only
  • GPU support is not available in the Java bindings

Preview API

onnxruntime-genai's Java API is still in preview upstream, so inference4j-genai may change between releases. Each genai upgrade is verified against real models before it ships.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
inference4j-genai depends on io.github.inference4j:onnxruntime-genai, a redistribution of Microsoft's official onnxruntime-genai Java release JAR on Maven Central:

inference4j onnxruntime-genai ONNX Runtime 0.13.0 0.17.0 1.28.0 0.10.1 0.15.2 1.26.0 0.10.0 0.12.0 1.23.0

One ONNX Runtime on the classpath

Since 0.13.0 the onnxruntime-genai JAR contains only the genai natives; it loads the ONNX Runtime native library from the regular com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime dependency that inference4j-core brings in. If you override the ONNX Runtime version yourself, keep it at or above the version in the table above.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
The two engines are complementary, and each has a clear job:

Use case Engine Why Chat and instruction LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Phi, Gemma, DeepSeek, …) onnxruntime-genai Upstream keeps pace with new architectures; we wrap them instead of re-implementing each one Vision-language (Phi-3.5 Vision) onnxruntime-genai Image preprocessing runs natively Speech-to-text with Whisper onnxruntime-genai Audio feature extraction runs natively Summarization, translation, grammar correction (Flan-T5, BART, MarianMT, CoEdIT) Native Encoder-decoder text models are not supported by onnxruntime-genai Small decoder models from a standard HuggingFace ONNX export (GPT-2, SmolLM2, TinyLlama) Native No genai export needed, and no extra native library

New LLM, vision-language and speech architectures will come through inference4j-genai. The native engine stays fully supported for encoder-decoder models and for anything onnxruntime-genai does not cover, and it remains the option when you want ONNX Runtime as your only native dependency.

docs.title: The autoregressive loop
docs.text:
A generative model doesn't produce its entire output in a single forward pass. It produces one token at a time. Each token is fed back into the model to produce the next one, forming a loop that continues until the model emits a stop token or reaches a maximum length.

flowchart TD
    A["Prompt tokens"] --> B["Forward pass"]
    B --> C["Next token"]
    C --> D{"Stop token?"}
    D -- No --> B
    D -- Yes --> E["Complete text"]

If you ask a model "What is Java?" and it generates a 50-token answer, the model runs 50 forward passes — one for each token in the response. This is why generation is orders of magnitude slower than classification or embedding.

docs.title: The KV cache
docs.text:
There's a problem with the naive loop above. Each forward pass computes attention over all previous tokens. Without optimization, generating token 50 would recompute attention over all 49 previous tokens from scratch — the same work done for tokens 1 through 49, repeated entirely.

The KV cache (key-value cache) solves this. During each forward pass, the model caches the intermediate key and value tensors from the attention layers. On the next pass, only the new token's attention needs to be computed — everything from previous tokens is read from the cache. This turns generation from O(n^2^) to O(n) in sequence length.

docs.title: Encoder-decoder models
docs.text:
The models described above (GPT-2, SmolLM2, Qwen2.5) are decoder-only — they process the entire input and output as a single sequence. Encoder-decoder models split the work into two parts:

  1. Encoder: processes the full input in a single forward pass, producing a rich representation of the input text
  2. Decoder: generates the output one token at a time, attending to the encoder's representation via cross-attention

This architecture is a natural fit for tasks where the input and output are structurally different — summarization (long article → short summary), translation (English → French), and grammar correction (broken text → fixed text).

flowchart TD
    A["Input text"] --> B["Encoder<br><small>single forward pass</small>"]
    B --> C["Encoder output<br><small>frozen representation</small>"]
    C --> D["Decoder step 1<br><small>cross-attention to encoder</small>"]
    D --> E["Token 1"]
    E --> F["Decoder step 2"]
    F --> G["Token 2"]
    G --> H["..."]
    H --> I{"Stop token?"}
    I -- No --> J["Decoder step N"]
    I -- Yes --> K["Complete output"]

docs.title: Two types of KV cache
docs.text:
Encoder-decoder models maintain two separate caches:

  • Cross-attention cache — computed once from the encoder output after the first decoder step, then frozen for the rest of generation. This is what lets the decoder "look at" the input without recomputing it.
  • Self-attention cache — grows with each decoder step, just like in decoder-only models. This cache stores the decoder's own previous states.

This split is the key architectural difference from decoder-only models, where there is only one KV cache that grows throughout generation.

docs.title: How the two approaches differ
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph native["Native generation (inference4j-core)"]
        direction LR
        N1["BPE tokenize<br><small>inference4j</small>"]
        N2["Forward pass + KV cache<br><small>ONNX Runtime</small>"]
        N3["Sample + decode<br><small>inference4j</small>"]
        N1 --> N2 --> N3
    end

    subgraph genai["onnxruntime-genai (inference4j-genai)"]
        direction LR
        G1["Tokenize + Generate loop + KV cache + Sampling + Decode<br><small>onnxruntime-genai (C++)</small>"]
    end

In native generation, inference4j handles tokenization, sampling, and decoding in Java while ONNX Runtime does the forward passes. In the genai path, the entire pipeline runs in onnxruntime-genai's native C++ layer.

docs.title: Native Text Generation
docs.text:
Generate text with GPT-2, SmolLM2, TinyLlama, Qwen2.5, Gemma 2, and other models using inference4j's native generation loop — no additional dependencies beyond ONNX Runtime.

OnnxTextGenerator is the single entry point for all natively-supported text generation models. Named presets provide one-liner access to popular models, and the generic builder supports custom models.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
// GPT-2 — completion model
try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.gpt2().maxNewTokens(50).build()) {
    System.out.println(gen.generate("Once upon a time").text());
}

// SmolLM2-360M — ChatML instruct model
try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.smolLM2().maxNewTokens(50).build()) {
    System.out.println(gen.generate("What is the capital of France?").text());
}

// TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat — Zephyr-style instruct model
try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.tinyLlama().maxNewTokens(100).build()) {
    System.out.println(gen.generate("Explain gravity").text());
}

// Qwen2.5-1.5B — ChatML instruct model
try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.qwen2().maxNewTokens(100).build()) {
    System.out.println(gen.generate("Explain gravity").text());
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.OnnxTextGenerator;

public class TextGeneration {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.qwen2()
                .maxNewTokens(100)
                .temperature(0.8f)
                .topK(50)
                .topP(0.9f)
                .build()) {

            GenerationResult result = gen.generate("The meaning of life is");

            System.out.println(result.text());
            System.out.printf("%d tokens in %,d ms%n",
                    result.generatedTokens(), result.duration().toMillis());
        }
    }
}

Enable sampling for better output

GPT-2 defaults to greedy decoding (temperature=0), which produces repetitive text. Set temperature, topK, and topP for more coherent output. Instruct models (SmolLM2, Qwen2.5) also benefit from sampling.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Pass a Consumer<String> to receive tokens as they are generated:

try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.smolLM2()
        .maxNewTokens(100)
        .temperature(0.8f)
        .topK(50)
        .build()) {
    gen.generate("Tell me a joke", token -> System.out.print(token));
}

The final GenerationResult is still returned after generation completes, containing the full text and timing information.

docs.title: Model presets
Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String Preset-dependent HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer — ONNX Runtime session options (e.g., thread count) .chatTemplate(ChatTemplate) ChatTemplate Preset-dependent Prompt formatting .addedToken(String) String Preset-dependent Register a special token for atomic encoding .tokenizerProvider(TokenizerProvider) TokenizerProvider GPT-2 BPE Tokenizer construction strategy (e.g., SentencePiece for Gemma) .maxNewTokens(int) int 256 Maximum number of tokens to generate .temperature(float) float 0.0 Sampling temperature (higher = more random) .topK(int) int 0 (disabled) Top-K sampling (keep K most probable tokens) .topP(float) float 0.0 (disabled) Nucleus sampling (keep tokens summing to P probability) .eosTokenId(int) int Auto-detected End-of-sequence token ID (loaded from config.json) .stopSequence(String) String — Stop sequence (can be called multiple times) .maxInputLength(int) int Model positions minus maxNewTokens Maximum prompt length in tokens .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Longer prompts: TRUNCATE keeps the chat template and the end of the message and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Prompt length

docs.title: Prompt length
docs.text:
The prompt and the generated tokens share the model's positions (max_position_embeddings or n_positions in config.json). The default prompt limit is therefore that number minus maxNewTokens, for example 1024 − 256 = 768 tokens for GPT-2 with the default maxNewTokens. If config.json declares no limit, prompts are not truncated.

Case Behavior Prompt within the limit Sent in full Prompt over the limit Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL)

docs.title: What truncation keeps
docs.text:
A decoder-only model answers only after the chat template's closing tokens (for ChatML, <|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n), and it continues from the end of its input. So when a prompt is too long, TRUNCATE keeps:

  1. the template's prefix, including any system prompt;
  2. the end of your message, as much as fits;
  3. the template's suffix, the cue for the model to answer.

The beginning of the message is dropped. A prompt without a chat template keeps its end. This matches how chat runtimes such as Ollama and llama.cpp drop the oldest context first.

For example, a long document followed by a question, cut to 80 tokens, still gets an answer:

try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.qwen2().maxInputLength(80).build()) {
    gen.generate(longDocument + "\n\nQuestion: What is the capital of France? Answer with one word.");
    // " Paris": the question and the template's closing tokens were kept
}

Before this behavior, the template's closing tokens were cut, and the model continued the document instead of answering. If the important part of your input is at the start, put the question last, or use FAIL and shorten the input yourself.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
GenerationResult is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The generated text promptTokens() int Number of tokens in the input prompt generatedTokens() int Number of tokens generated duration() Duration Wall-clock generation time

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
OnnxTextGenerator uses inference4j's native generation engine. The entire autoregressive loop — tokenization, KV cache management, sampling, and decoding — runs in Java, with only the forward passes delegated to ONNX Runtime.

flowchart TD
    A["User prompt"] --> B["Tokenize<br><small>inference4j</small>"]
    B --> C["Forward pass + KV cache<br><small>ONNX Runtime</small>"]
    C --> D["Sample next token<br><small>inference4j</small>"]
    D --> E{"Stop?"}
    E -- No --> C
    E -- Yes --> F["Decode tokens<br><small>inference4j</small>"]
    F --> G["GenerationResult"]

See the introduction for a detailed explanation of the autoregressive loop, KV cache, and how native generation compares to onnxruntime-genai.

docs.title: Custom models
docs.text:
Use OnnxTextGenerator.builder() for any BPE-based causal LM exported to ONNX with KV cache:

try (var gen = OnnxTextGenerator.builder()
        .modelId("my-org/my-model")
        .addedToken("<|special_start|>")
        .addedToken("<|special_end|>")
        .chatTemplate(msg -> "<|user|>" + msg + "<|assistant|>")
        .temperature(0.7f)
        .maxNewTokens(100)
        .build()) {
    gen.generate("Hello", token -> System.out.print(token));
}

By default, the builder uses GPT-2-style BPE (vocab.json + merges.txt). For SentencePiece models (Gemma, LLaMA, TinyLlama), use .tokenizerProvider(SentencePieceBpeTokenizer.provider()) which reads tokenizer.json instead.

The model directory must contain model.onnx and config.json, plus the tokenizer files required by the provider.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use temperature(0.8f), topK(50), topP(0.9f) to avoid degenerate repetition from greedy decoding.
  • Lower maxNewTokens for demos or quick tests — it directly controls how many forward passes run.
  • Reuse OnnxTextGenerator instances across prompts — each one holds the model and tokenizer in memory.
  • Models download on first use and are cached in ~/.cache/inference4j/.

docs.title: Phi-3.5 Vision
docs.text:
Ask questions about images and get text answers using Microsoft's Phi-3.5 Vision model.

See the overview for background on how autoregressive generation differs from single-pass inference.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var vision = VisionLanguageModel.builder()
        .model(ModelSources.phi3Vision())
        .build()) {
    GenerationResult result = vision.generate(
            new VisionInput(Path.of("cat.jpg"), "Describe this image."));
    System.out.println(result.text());
}

The image shows a close-up of an orange tabby cat with a white collar.
The cat's eyes are green, and it has a neutral expression. The background
is blurred, with hints of a red object and a green plant.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.genai.ModelSources;
import io.github.inference4j.genai.vision.VisionInput;
import io.github.inference4j.genai.vision.VisionLanguageModel;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class ImageDescription {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path image = Path.of("cat.jpg");

        try (var vision = VisionLanguageModel.builder()
                .model(ModelSources.phi3Vision())
                .build()) {

            // Describe an image
            GenerationResult description = vision.generate(
                    new VisionInput(image, "Describe this image."));
            System.out.println(description.text());

            // Ask a question about it
            GenerationResult answer = vision.generate(
                    new VisionInput(image, "What colors are prominent in this image?"));
            System.out.println(answer.text());
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Pass a Consumer<String> to receive tokens as they are generated:

try (var vision = VisionLanguageModel.builder()
        .model(ModelSources.phi3Vision())
        .build()) {
    vision.generate(
            new VisionInput(Path.of("cat.jpg"), "Describe this image."),
            token -> System.out.print(token));
}

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .model(GenerativeModel) GenerativeModel — Preconfigured model from ModelSources .modelId(String) String — HuggingFace model ID (requires .chatTemplate()) .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .chatTemplate(ChatTemplate) ChatTemplate — Prompt formatting (must include <\|image_1\|> placeholder) .maxLength(int) int 4096 Maximum total sequence length (input image tokens + output tokens) .temperature(double) double 0.0 Sampling temperature (0 = greedy) .topK(int) int 0 (disabled) Top-K sampling .topP(double) double 0.0 (disabled) Nucleus sampling .intraOpThreads(int) int all cores Threads per ONNX Runtime session. Applied as an overlay on the model's genai_config.json; the files on disk are not changed

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Description generate(VisionInput) Generate text from an image and prompt generate(VisionInput, Consumer) Generate with token streaming

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Phi-3.5 Vision is a decoder-only vision-language model. Unlike Whisper (encoder-decoder), it interleaves image tokens with text tokens in a single sequence:

  1. The image goes through a CLIP ViT encoder to produce visual embeddings
  2. An MLP projector maps visual embeddings into the language model's token space
  3. The Phi-3 Mini decoder processes interleaved image + text tokens autoregressively
flowchart LR
    A["Image file"] --> B["onnxruntime-genai<br>CLIP encoder → projector → Phi-3 decoder"]
    C["Text prompt"] --> B
    B --> D["GenerationResult"]

All heavy lifting — image preprocessing, vision encoding, embedding projection, autoregressive decoding, KV cache — is handled natively by onnxruntime-genai.

docs.title: Custom models
docs.text:
For a custom vision-language model, provide a model source and chat template:

try (var vision = VisionLanguageModel.builder()
        .modelId("my-org/my-vision-model")
        .chatTemplate(msg ->
                "<|user|>\n<|image_1|>\n" + msg + "\n<|end|>\n<|assistant|>\n")
        .build()) {
    vision.generate(new VisionInput(Path.of("photo.jpg"), "Describe this image."));
}

The chat template must include <|image_1|> where the image embeddings should be inserted. The MultiModalProcessor handles the substitution internally.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• temperature(0.0) (default) gives deterministic, greedy decoding — best for factual descriptions.
  • Use higher maxLength for detailed descriptions and lower values for short answers.
  • The model downloads ~3.3 GB on first use (INT4 quantized).
  • Reuse VisionLanguageModel instances — each one holds three ONNX models in memory (vision encoder, embedding projector, text decoder).

docs.title: Text Generation
docs.text:
Generate text with decoder-only language models like Phi-4-mini, Qwen3, SmolLM3 and DeepSeek-R1, with built-in streaming support.

See the overview for background on how autoregressive generation differs from single-pass inference.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var generator = TextGenerator.builder()
        .model(ModelSources.phi3Mini())
        .build()) {
    System.out.println(generator.generate("What is Java?").text());
}

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Preset Model Size (INT4) License Notes ModelSources.qwen3_0_6B() Qwen3-0.6B ~0.4 GB Apache-2.0 Smallest; multilingual ModelSources.deepSeekR1_1_5B() DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B ~1 GB MIT Reasoning: writes its thinking before the answer ModelSources.smolLM3_3B() SmolLM3-3B ~2 GB Apache-2.0 ModelSources.phi3Mini() Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct ~2.7 GB MIT ModelSources.phi4Mini() Phi-4-mini-instruct ~4.9 GB MIT 128K-token context

Qwen3 and SmolLM3 can also "think" (write out their reasoning in a <think> block before answering). Their presets use the models' non-thinking mode, so they answer directly. For thinking mode, pass your own ChatTemplate without the empty <think></think> block (and, for SmolLM3, with /think in the system prompt).

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.genai.ModelSources;
import io.github.inference4j.genai.nlp.TextGenerator;

public class TextGeneration {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var generator = TextGenerator.builder()
                .model(ModelSources.phi3Mini())
                .maxLength(200)
                .temperature(0.7)
                .build()) {

            GenerationResult result = generator.generate("What is Java in one sentence?");

            System.out.println(result.text());
            System.out.printf("%d tokens in %,d ms%n",
                    result.generatedTokens(), result.duration().toMillis());
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Pass a Consumer<String> to receive tokens as they are generated:

try (var generator = TextGenerator.builder()
        .model(ModelSources.deepSeekR1_1_5B())
        .maxLength(200)
        .build()) {
    generator.generate("Explain recursion in simple terms.", token -> System.out.print(token));
}

The final GenerationResult is still returned after generation completes, containing the full text and timing information.

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text:
chat generates the next assistant message of a conversation, with system and earlier assistant messages:

GenerationResult result = gen.chat(List.of(
        ChatMessage.system("Answer in one sentence."),
        ChatMessage.user("What is Java?")));

chat(List<ChatMessage>, Consumer<String>) streams the answer. The conversation is formatted with the chat template's conversation format; see Chat templates. To use a TextGenerator from LangChain4j, see Chat model.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .model(GenerativeModel) GenerativeModel — Preconfigured model from ModelSources .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource — Custom model source (requires .chatTemplate()) .chatTemplate(ChatTemplate) ChatTemplate — Prompt formatting for custom models .maxLength(int) int 1024 Maximum sequence length in tokens, prompt plus generated text. onnxruntime-genai reserves memory for the key/value cache up front based on this value (see Tips) .temperature(double) double 1.0 Sampling temperature (higher = more random) .topK(int) int 0 (disabled) Top-K sampling (keep K most probable tokens) .topP(double) double 0.0 (disabled) Nucleus sampling (keep tokens summing to P probability) .maxNewTokens(int) int no limit of its own Maximum number of tokens to generate per call, not counting the prompt. Generation also stops at maxLength .repetitionPenalty(double) double model default Values above 1 make repeated tokens less likely .stopSequence(String) String none Ends generation when the string appears. The stop sequence and anything after it are left out of the result and are not streamed. Can be called several times .intraOpThreads(int) int all cores Threads per ONNX Runtime session. Applied as an overlay on the model's genai_config.json; the files on disk are not changed

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
GenerationResult is a record with three fields:

Field Type Description text() String The generated text promptTokens() int Number of tokens in the input prompt, after the chat template is applied generatedTokens() int Number of tokens generated duration() Duration Wall-clock generation time

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
TextGenerator formats the prompt using the model's chat template, then delegates to onnxruntime-genai for tokenization, the autoregressive generation loop, and decoding.

flowchart LR
    A["User prompt"] --> B["ChatTemplate<br>format prompt"]
    B --> C["onnxruntime-genai<br>tokenize → generate → decode"]
    C --> D["GenerationResult"]

See the overview for a detailed explanation of the generation loop, KV cache, and why this architecture differs from single-pass wrappers.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Generation speed scales with model size. DeepSeek-R1 (1.5B) is noticeably faster than Phi-3 (3.8B) on the same hardware.
  • Keep maxLength close to what you need. It bounds the prompt plus the answer, and onnxruntime-genai allocates the key/value cache for the full maxLength up front. For SmolLM3-3B we measured a peak of 2.8 GB at maxLength(256), but 12.3 GB at its full 65,536-token context.
  • With long prompts, such as retrieved documents, set maxNewTokens to bound the answer. maxLength alone counts the prompt too, so a longer prompt leaves less room for the answer.
  • temperature below 1.0 gives more focused output; above 1.0 gives more varied output.
  • Reuse TextGenerator instances across prompts — each one holds the model in memory.

docs.title: Whisper Speech-to-Text
docs.text:
Transcribe and translate speech using OpenAI's Whisper models, with automatic chunking for long audio.

See the overview for background on how autoregressive generation differs from single-pass inference.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Model ID Parameters Size 11 s clip on CPU* inference4j/whisper-tiny-genai 39M ~225 MB ~0.1 s inference4j/whisper-small-genai 244M ~1.1 GB ~0.5 s

* Measured on an Apple M4 Pro. Both are FP32 exports made with onnxruntime-genai's model builder, and download on first use.

small transcribes noticeably better, including punctuation such as commas; tiny is the choice when size and speed matter most.

Verified for English transcription

Our tests cover English transcription. Whisper also supports 98 other languages and translation to English (shown below), but we have not verified those yet.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var whisper = WhisperSpeechModel.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai")
        .build()) {
    System.out.println(whisper.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav")).text());
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.genai.audio.WhisperSpeechModel;
import io.github.inference4j.audio.Transcription;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class WhisperTranscription {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var whisper = WhisperSpeechModel.builder()
                .modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai")
                .build()) {

            Transcription result = whisper.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav"));
            System.out.println(result.text());
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Translation
docs.text:
Whisper can translate speech from any supported language into English:

try (var whisper = WhisperSpeechModel.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai")
        .language("fr")
        .task(WhisperTask.TRANSLATE)
        .build()) {
    Transcription result = whisper.transcribe(Path.of("french-audio.wav"));
    System.out.println(result.text());  // English translation
}

docs.title: From raw audio data
docs.text:
If you already have audio samples as a float array:

try (var whisper = WhisperSpeechModel.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai")
        .build()) {
    float[] samples = loadAudioSamples();
    Transcription result = whisper.transcribe(samples, 16000);
    System.out.println(result.text());
}

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String — HuggingFace model ID (required) .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .language(String) String "en" Source language code (e.g., "fr", "de", "ja") .task(WhisperTask) WhisperTask TRANSCRIBE TRANSCRIBE or TRANSLATE (to English) .maxLength(int) int 448 Maximum number of tokens to generate per chunk .temperature(double) double 0.0 Sampling temperature (0 = greedy) .topK(int) int 0 (disabled) Top-K sampling .topP(double) double 0.0 (disabled) Nucleus sampling .intraOpThreads(int) int all cores Threads per ONNX Runtime session. Applied as an overlay on the model's genai_config.json; the files on disk are not changed

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
Transcription is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The transcribed or translated text segments() List<Segment> Timed segments: empty for Whisper on its own, which runs without timestamps; one per piece when wrapped in SegmentedSpeechRecognizer

Each Segment contains:

Field Type Description text() String Segment text startTime() float Start time in seconds endTime() float End time in seconds

docs.title: Long audio
docs.text:
Whisper sees 30 seconds of audio per pass; this is a property of the model, not of inference4j. On its own, WhisperSpeechModel handles longer audio by cutting it every 30 seconds. Those cuts land in the middle of words and sentences, and Whisper then drops or repeats text around them, sometimes losing a whole 30-second chunk.

For recordings longer than 30 seconds, wrap the model in SegmentedSpeechRecognizer, which cuts at pauses found by voice activity detection:

try (SpeechRecognizer recognizer = new SegmentedSpeechRecognizer(
        WhisperSpeechModel.builder().modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai").build(),
        SileroVadDetector.builder().build())) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav")).text());
}
Word error rate (lower is better) Cut every 30 s SegmentedSpeechRecognizer HF transformers chunked HF transformers sequential whisper-tiny 13.2% 6.1% 6.1% 6.5% whisper-small 11.7% 3.7% 3.7% 3.9%

Measured on the 11 talks of the TED-LIUM long-form test set (148 minutes), with Whisper's standard English text normalizer. The two right-hand columns run the same models through the HuggingFace transformers reference implementation's long-form strategies (30-second chunks with 5-second overlap, and OpenAI's timestamp-driven sequential decoding). The voice activity detection adds processing time: 12% with whisper-small (302 s instead of 270 s for all 11 talks on an Apple M4 Pro CPU) and 40% with the much faster whisper-tiny (74 s instead of 53 s).

Cutting at pauses roughly halves tiny's error rate and cuts small's by two thirds, matching the reference implementation. See Long recordings for how the cuts are chosen.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Unlike Wav2Vec2 (single-pass CTC), Whisper is an autoregressive encoder-decoder model. The audio is encoded into a mel spectrogram, then the decoder generates text tokens one at a time.

flowchart LR
    A["Audio file"] --> B["onnxruntime-genai<br>mel spectrogram → encoder → decoder loop"]
    B --> C["Transcription"]

All heavy lifting — mel spectrogram computation, encoder forward pass, autoregressive decoding and the KV cache — is handled natively by onnxruntime-genai's C++ layer.

docs.title: Whisper vs Wav2Vec2
docs.text: Wav2Vec2 Whisper Architecture CTC (single-pass) Encoder-decoder (autoregressive) Speed Fast Slower (token-by-token) Accuracy Good on clean speech Better on diverse audio Languages English (default model) 99 languages Translation No Yes (to English) Module inference4j-core inference4j-genai

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use WhisperTask.TRANSLATE to translate any language to English in a single step.
  • Smaller models (tiny, base) are faster but less accurate. The small model is a good balance.
  • temperature(0.0) (default) gives deterministic, greedy decoding — best for transcription accuracy.
  • Reuse WhisperSpeechModel instances — each one holds the model in memory.
  • For short, clean English audio where speed matters, Wav2Vec2 may be a better fit.

docs.title: What is ONNX?
docs.text:
ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open standard for representing machine learning models. A model trained in any framework — PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX — can be exported to a single .onnx file that captures the model's architecture and weights in a framework-independent format.

ONNX Runtime is a high-performance engine that runs these .onnx files. It provides hardware acceleration (CPU, GPU, CoreML, CUDA) and has native bindings for many languages, including Java.

inference4j builds on top of the ONNX Runtime Java API, adding preprocessing, postprocessing, and model management so you don't have to work with tensors directly.

Useful links:

  • ONNX specification
  • ONNX Runtime documentation
  • ONNX Runtime Java API
  • HuggingFace ONNX models

docs.title: The three-stage pipeline
docs.text:
Almost every inference task follows the same pattern:

flowchart LR
    Input["Java Object<br>String, BufferedImage, Path"]

    subgraph inference4j["inference4j wrapper"]
        Pre["Preprocess"]
        Infer["Infer"]
        Post["Postprocess"]
        Pre --> Infer --> Post
    end

    Output["Java Object<br>List of Classification, Transcription, ..."]

    Input --> Pre
    Post --> Output

docs.title: 1. Preprocess
docs.text:
Converts Java objects into tensors — the multi-dimensional arrays that models consume.

What this looks like depends on the domain:

Domain Input Preprocessing NLP String Tokenize text → input_ids + attention_mask tensors Vision BufferedImage Resize, normalize pixels, rearrange channels → float tensor Audio Path (WAV file) Load samples, resample to 16kHz, normalize → float tensor

This is where most of the model-specific knowledge lives: normalization constants, tokenizer vocabulary, expected input dimensions, channel layout (NCHW vs NHWC).

docs.title: 2. Infer
docs.text: A single forward pass through the ONNX model via ONNX Runtime. Tensors in, tensors out. This stage is model-agnostic — ONNX Runtime handles it regardless of which framework trained the model.

docs.title: 3. Postprocess
docs.text:
Converts raw output tensors back into meaningful Java objects.

Task Raw output Postprocessing Result Classification Float array (logits) Softmax → top-K → label mapping List<Classification> Object detection Float array (boxes + scores) NMS → coordinate rescaling → label mapping List<Detection> Speech-to-text Float array (per-frame logits) CTC greedy decode → character joining Transcription Text detection Pixel-level heatmap Thresholding → connected components → bounding boxes List<TextRegion>

docs.title: What is a Tensor?
docs.text:
A tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers. If you're familiar with Java arrays:

  • A float is a 0-dimensional tensor (a scalar)
  • A float[] is a 1-dimensional tensor (a vector)
  • A float[][] is a 2-dimensional tensor (a matrix)
  • A float[][][] is a 3-dimensional tensor

ML models consume and produce tensors with specific shapes. For example, a ResNet image classification model expects an input tensor with shape [1, 3, 224, 224] — that's 1 image, 3 color channels (RGB), 224 pixels tall, 224 pixels wide. The shape convention ([batch, channels, height, width] vs [batch, height, width, channels]) depends on the model's origin framework.

inference4j handles all tensor creation and interpretation internally. You never need to construct a tensor yourself.

docs.title: Example: what happens when you classify an image
docs.text:
try (var classifier = ResNetClassifier.builder().build()) {
    List<Classification> results = classifier.classify(Path.of("cat.jpg"));
}

Behind that single classify() call:

flowchart TD
    A["cat.jpg (Path)"]

    subgraph preprocess ["Preprocess"]
        B["Load BufferedImage"]
        C["Resize to 224x224"]
        D["Normalize pixels<br>mean: 0.485, 0.456, 0.406<br>std: 0.229, 0.224, 0.225"]
        E["Arrange into NCHW layout<br>shape: 1, 3, 224, 224"]
        B --> C --> D --> E
    end

    subgraph infer ["Infer"]
        F["ONNX Runtime forward pass"]
        G["Raw logits — shape: 1, 1000"]
        F --> G
    end

    subgraph postprocess ["Postprocess"]
        H["Softmax to probabilities"]
        I["Top-K selection"]
        J["Map indices to ImageNet labels"]
        H --> I --> J
    end

    K["List of Classification<br>tabby cat: 0.87, ..."]

    A --> B
    E --> F
    G --> H
    J --> K

All of this — the resizing, normalization, channel layout, softmax, label mapping — is encoded in the ResNetClassifier wrapper. A different model (say, EfficientNet) has different normalization constants, a different input layout (NHWC instead of NCHW), and may or may not need softmax applied. Each wrapper knows its model's requirements.

docs.title: Beyond single-pass: autoregressive generation
docs.text:
The three-stage pipeline above covers single-pass models — those that produce their entire output in one forward pass. Classification, embedding, detection, and speech-to-text all follow this pattern.

Text generation works differently. A generative model produces output one token at a time, feeding each token back into the model to produce the next one. This autoregressive loop, along with KV cache management and token sampling, requires a fundamentally different architecture that doesn't fit the preprocess-infer-postprocess pipeline.

inference4j handles this in two ways:

  • OnnxTextGenerator (in inference4j-core) — a pure ONNX Runtime generation loop with KV cache management, sampling, and streaming. Supports GPT-2, SmolLM2, Qwen2.5, and custom BPE-based models. No additional dependencies.
  • inference4j-genai — backed by onnxruntime-genai for larger models (Phi-3, DeepSeek-R1, Phi-3.5 Vision). See the Generative AI section for details.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Browse use cases to see the single-pass wrappers in action
  • Generative AI for autoregressive text generation
  • Adding a Wrapper explains the internals for contributors

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Java 17 or higher
  • ONNX Runtime 1.28.0 (included transitively via inference4j-core)

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
inference4j-core is the only dependency you need — it includes all task wrappers, preprocessing, and tokenizers.

GradleMaven 
implementation 'io.github.inference4j:inference4j-core:${inference4jVersion}'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>${inference4jVersion}</version>
</dependency>

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
For text generation (Phi-3, DeepSeek-R1, etc.), add inference4j-genai instead:

GradleMaven 
implementation 'io.github.inference4j:inference4j-genai'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-genai</artifactId>
</dependency>

This is a separate module backed by onnxruntime-genai. See the Generative AI guide for details.

inference4j-genai includes inference4j-core, so the task wrappers are available too.

ONNX Runtime version

onnxruntime-genai loads ONNX Runtime from the regular ONNX Runtime dependency that inference4j-core brings in. If you override the ONNX Runtime version, keep it at or above the one listed in Generative AI → Versions.

docs.title: JVM flags
docs.text:
ONNX Runtime requires native access. Add this flag to your JVM arguments:

--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED

Or, if you're on the module path:

--enable-native-access=com.microsoft.onnxruntime

docs.title: Setting JVM flags in Gradle
docs.text:
tasks.withType(JavaExec).configureEach {
    jvmArgs '--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED'
}

tasks.withType(Test).configureEach {
    jvmArgs '--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED'
}

docs.title: Spring Boot
docs.text:
For Spring Boot applications, use the starter instead. It requires Spring Boot 4.0 or later as of inference4j 0.11.0 — see the Spring Boot guide if you are still on Boot 3.

GradleMaven 
implementation 'io.github.inference4j:inference4j-spring-boot-starter:${inference4jVersion}'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>${inference4jVersion}</version>
</dependency>

See the Spring Boot guide for configuration details.

docs.title: LangChain4j
docs.text:
To use inference4j models through LangChain4j's interfaces (EmbeddingModel, ScoringModel, DocumentParser, DocumentTransformer, InputGuardrail), add the adapter module. It includes inference4j-core. LangChain4j is supplied by the application.

GradleMaven 
implementation 'io.github.inference4j:inference4j-langchain4j:${inference4jVersion}'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-langchain4j</artifactId>
    <version>${inference4jVersion}</version>
</dependency>

See the LangChain4j guide.

docs.title: Pre-release snapshots (JitPack)
docs.text:
To try features merged to main before they reach Maven Central, build them through JitPack. JitPack serves every module under the com.github.inference4j.inference4j group, at version main-SNAPSHOT (the latest commit on main) or at a commit hash (a fixed build, recommended for anything you want to reproduce):

GradleMaven 
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven { url 'https://jitpack.io' }
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'com.github.inference4j.inference4j:inference4j-core:main-SNAPSHOT'
}

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>jitpack.io</id>
        <url>https://jitpack.io</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.github.inference4j.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>main-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The other modules work the same way (inference4j-genai, inference4j-runtime, inference4j-spring-boot-starter); their dependencies on each other resolve from JitPack too.

Snapshots

  • Don't mix JitPack and Maven Central coordinates for inference4j modules in one build: the two groups would put the same classes on the classpath twice.
  • The first request for a new commit starts a build on JitPack, which can take a few minutes.
  • Gradle caches -SNAPSHOT versions for 24 hours; run with --refresh-dependencies to pick up a newer commit sooner.
  • Snapshots are not releases: APIs can change before the next version ships.

docs.title: GPU support
docs.text:
The default dependency includes CPU and CoreML (macOS) support. For CUDA (Linux/Windows), swap the ONNX Runtime dependency:

GradleMaven 
implementation('io.github.inference4j:inference4j-core:${inference4jVersion}') {
    exclude group: 'com.microsoft.onnxruntime', module: 'onnxruntime'
}
implementation 'com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime_gpu:${onnxruntimeVersion}'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.inference4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>inference4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>${inference4jVersion}</version>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>com.microsoft.onnxruntime</groupId>
            <artifactId>onnxruntime</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.microsoft.onnxruntime</groupId>
    <artifactId>onnxruntime_gpu</artifactId>
    <version>${onnxruntimeVersion}</version>
</dependency>

See the Hardware Acceleration guide for usage details.

docs.title: Your first model in 3 lines
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.DistilBertTextClassifier;

public class QuickStart {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder().build()) {
            System.out.println(classifier.classify("inference4j makes AI in Java easy!"));
            // [TextClassification[label=POSITIVE, confidence=0.9998]]
        }
    }
}

That's it. The model downloads automatically on first run (~260MB, cached in ~/.cache/inference4j/). No Python, no manual downloads, no tensor wrangling.

docs.title: What happens under the hood
docs.text:
When you call builder().build():

  1. Model resolution — The builder resolves the default model ID (inference4j/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english) using HuggingFaceModelSource, which downloads the ONNX model, vocabulary, and config files to ~/.cache/inference4j/
  2. Session creation — An ONNX Runtime InferenceSession is created with default session options
  3. Tokenizer setup — A WordPieceTokenizer is loaded from the downloaded vocab.txt

When you call classify(text):

  1. Preprocessing — The text is tokenized into input IDs and attention mask tensors
  2. Inference — Tensors are passed to the ONNX Runtime session for a single forward pass
  3. Postprocessing — Raw logits are transformed via softmax into labeled classifications

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.vision.ResNetClassifier;

try (var classifier = ResNetClassifier.builder().build()) {
    var results = classifier.classify(Path.of("cat.jpg"));
    results.forEach(c ->
        System.out.printf("%s: %.2f%%%n", c.label(), c.confidence() * 100));
}

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.audio.Wav2Vec2Recognizer;

try (var recognizer = Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build()) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav")).text());
}

docs.title: Customizing the builder
docs.text:
Every model wrapper follows the same builder pattern:

try (var classifier = ResNetClassifier.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/resnet50-v1-7")     // override default model
        .sessionOptions(opts -> opts.addCoreML())  // hardware acceleration
        .defaultTopK(3)                            // return top 3 predictions
        .build()) {
    classifier.classify(Path.of("cat.jpg"));
}

Common builder methods available on all wrappers:

Method Description .modelId(String) Override the default HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) Use a custom model source (e.g., LocalModelSource) .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) Configure ONNX Runtime options (GPU, threads)

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Browse the Use Cases for detailed examples of each capability
  • See Hardware Acceleration for GPU and CoreML setup
  • Check Supported Models for all available models

docs.title: Hardware Acceleration
docs.text: inference4j supports GPU and hardware acceleration via ONNX Runtime execution providers. The .sessionOptions() API is available on every model wrapper.

docs.title: CoreML (macOS)
docs.text:
CoreML is bundled in the standard ONNX Runtime dependency on macOS — no additional setup needed.

try (var classifier = ResNetClassifier.builder()
        .sessionOptions(opts -> opts.addCoreML())
        .build()) {
    classifier.classify(Path.of("cat.jpg"));
}

docs.title: CoreML results can differ from CPU results
docs.text:
addCoreML() converts the model to CoreML's older NeuralNetwork format. CoreML runs it on the Apple GPU or Neural Engine with reduced numeric precision, so scores shift slightly, and for some models the output changes. Models that pick their top results inside the graph, such as YOLO26's 300 proposals, are the most affected: a small change in scores changes which boxes survive.

The newer MLProgram format keeps CPU-level accuracy for the models that support it:

try (var detector = DetrDetector.builder()
        .sessionOptions(opts -> opts.addCoreML(Map.of("ModelFormat", "MLProgram")))
        .build()) {
    detector.detect(Path.of("street.jpg"));
}

Other CoreML provider options, such as MLComputeUnits (CPUAndGPU, CPUAndNeuralEngine, ALL), go in the same map; see the ONNX Runtime CoreML documentation.

Not every model speeds up, and not every model converts. Measured with inference4j on Apple silicon (ONNX Runtime 1.28, warm runs, per image):

Model CPU addCoreML() (NeuralNetwork) MLProgram CRAFT (CraftTextDetector) 587 ms 214 ms, same regions fails to load YOLO26n (Yolo26Detector) 26 ms 15 ms, different detections 25 ms, same as CPU D-FINE small (DetrDetector) 57 ms 112 ms, scores within 0.01 102 ms, same as CPU RT-DETRv2 (DetrDetector.rtDetrV2()) 106 ms 122 ms, some labels differ 98 ms, same as CPU D-FINE nano (DetrDetector.dfineNano()) 32 ms fails when run fails to load PP-OCRv6 small (OcrPipeline) ~400 ms ~860 ms not measured

Small, CPU-optimized models (YOLO26n, D-FINE, PP-OCRv6) gain little or nothing from CoreML: ONNX Runtime splits them into many CoreML and CPU pieces, and copying data between them costs more than the GPU saves. Large convolutional networks such as CRAFT gain the most. Measure your model on your hardware, and compare its output with the CPU's, before switching.

docs.title: CUDA (Linux/Windows)
docs.text:
For NVIDIA GPU acceleration, swap the ONNX Runtime dependency:

GradleMaven 
implementation('io.github.inference4j:inference4j-core:${inference4jVersion}') {
    exclude group: 'com.microsoft.onnxruntime', module: 'onnxruntime'
}
implementation 'com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime_gpu:${onnxruntimeVersion}'

<dependency>
