docs.text: Find the lines of text in an image and read them, locally, with PaddleOCR's PP-OCRv6 models. Each line comes back with its text, a confidence and its outline in the image, in reading order.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var ocr = OcrPipeline.builder().build()) {
    for (TextLine line : ocr.read(Path.of("receipt.jpg"))) {
        System.out.println(line.text());
    }
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.vision.OcrPipeline;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.TextLine;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

public class ReadReceipt {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var ocr = OcrPipeline.builder()
                .minConfidence(0.5f)          // drop lines the recognizer is unsure about
                .build()) {
            List<TextLine> lines = ocr.read(Path.of("receipt.jpg"));
            for (TextLine line : lines) {
                System.out.printf("%-40s %.2f  at %s%n",
                    line.text(), line.confidence(), line.region().box());
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Recognition models read one line at a time: they resize their input to a fixed height (48 pixels), so a whole page given to them directly produces nothing useful. OcrPipeline therefore runs two models:

  1. Detect: PaddleTextDetector finds every line of text, including rotated ones, as a four-corner outline.
  2. Crop: QuadCrop cuts each outline out of the image as an upright rectangle (a perspective transform); a crop much taller than wide, such as vertical text, is turned 90°.
  3. Recognize: PaddleTextRecognizer reads each crop and returns its text and confidence.

Lines are returned top to bottom, then left to right.

docs.title: Models
OcrPipeline.builder()
docs.text:
Method Type Default Description .detector(TextDetector) TextDetector PaddleTextDetector.small() Finds the text regions .recognizer(TextRecognizer) TextRecognizer PaddleTextRecognizer.small() Reads each region .minConfidence(float) float 0 Lines read with a lower confidence are left out; empty lines always are

Closing the pipeline closes both stages.

docs.title: PaddleTextDetector
docs.text:
Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/pp-ocrv6-small-det HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .threshold(float) float 0.3 Probability above which a pixel of the model's map counts as text .boxThreshold(float) float 0.6 Minimum mean probability inside a line for it to be kept .unclipRatio(float) float 1.5 How far lines are expanded beyond the model's shrunken text core .maxCandidates(int) int 3000 Maximum candidate areas examined per image .minSide(int) int 64 Images with a shorter side below this are scaled up .maxSide(int) int 4000 Images with a longer side above this are scaled down

The defaults are those of the paddleocr Python package's OCR pipeline. Images otherwise keep their own size (rounded to multiples of 32), so small text in large images stays readable, at the cost of time on large images.

docs.title: PaddleTextRecognizer
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/pp-ocrv6-small-rec HuggingFace model ID; the directory needs model.onnx and inference.yml .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config

docs.title: Result types
docs.text:
TextLine is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The recognized text confidence() float The recognizer's confidence (0.0 to 1.0): the mean probability of the characters read region() TextRegion Where the line is: box() (axis-aligned) and polygon() (four corners, clockwise from the top-left)

TextRecognizer.recognize(BufferedImage) returns a RecognizedText(text, confidence) for one line image.

docs.title: Using the stages separately
docs.text:
The detector and the recognizer are ordinary tasks, so each can be used alone, for example to find where text is without reading it, or to read crops you already have:

try (var detector = PaddleTextDetector.small().build();
     var recognizer = PaddleTextRecognizer.small().build()) {
    for (TextRegion region : detector.detect(page)) {
        RecognizedText text = recognizer.recognize(QuadCrop.crop(page, region.polygon()));
    }
}

CraftTextDetector also fits OcrPipeline.builder().detector(...). CRAFT finds words or word groups rather than whole lines, so each word is read separately (see Text Detection).

docs.title: Measured accuracy
docs.text:
On five test pages (a document with a rotated line, a slightly rotated JPEG receipt, colored signage with a tilted line, a small-font screenshot, and a blurred, noisy scan: 31 lines in total), with known ground truth:

Preset Character accuracy Word accuracy Median time per page small() 100% 100% 133 ms tiny() 99.8% 98.6% 84 ms

Times are on a laptop CPU with four ONNX Runtime threads, for pages of 900 × 420 to 1200 × 820 pixels.

inference4j reproduces PaddleOCR's own processing step by step, including OpenCV's integer and single-precision rounding, which decides where box edges fall:

  • Against PaddleOCR's Python processing on the same ONNX models: identical text on all 31 lines, box corners identical or within one pixel, confidences within 0.0004.
  • Against the paddleocr package: identical text on all 31 lines. That package runs Paddle's own inference engine on Paddle-format weights, so its boxes differ by up to a few pixels and its confidences by a few hundredths.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• No orientation correction. Upside-down lines and rotated pages are not turned upright; PaddleOCR's optional orientation classifiers are not included.
  • Printed text. Handwriting is better served by TrOCR (#128).
  • Lines, not layout. Columns, tables and paragraphs are not reconstructed; lines come back in reading order.

docs.title: Pose Detection
docs.text:
Find the people in an image and the position of their body joints (also called pose estimation or keypoint detection). Each person comes back as a Pose: the person's box and score, plus 17 keypoints (nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles) in the image's pixel coordinates.

Typical uses: counting exercise repetitions and checking form from joint angles, posture and ergonomics scoring, sports and dance analytics, and storing skeletons instead of images where privacy matters.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (PoseDetector detector = RtmoPoseDetector.builder().build()) {      // RTMO-s, COCO only
    List<Pose> poses = detector.detect(Path.of("gym.jpg"));
    Keypoint wrist = poses.get(0).keypoint(CocoJoint.LEFT_WRIST);
}

docs.title: Choose a model
docs.text:
Preset Model Weights license Training data COCO keypoint AP (authors) ONNX size CPU latency* RtmoPoseDetector.s() (default) RTMO-s Apache-2.0 COCO 67.7 40 MB 43 ms RtmoPoseDetector.m() RTMO-m Apache-2.0 COCO 70.9 89 MB 91 ms RtmoPoseDetector.l() RTMO-l Apache-2.0 COCO 72.4 176 MB 155 ms

*Mean per image over seven COCO photos (640 × 640 input) on a laptop CPU with four ONNX Runtime threads, measured with inference4j. AP figures come from the RTMO authors (COCO val2017); inference4j has not re-measured them.

  • Start with RTMO-s: the smallest and fastest.
  • RTMO-m or RTMO-l when accuracy matters more than speed, for example small or distant people.

RTMO is a one-stage model: one run finds every person and their joints, so the cost does not grow with the number of people in the image.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
The angle at a joint is the building block of repetition counters and posture checks:

import io.github.inference4j.vision.CocoJoint;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.ImageAnnotator;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.Pose;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.PoseDetector;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.RtmoPoseDetector;
import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

public class PoseDetection {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        BufferedImage image = ImageIO.read(Path.of("squat.jpg").toFile());

        try (PoseDetector detector = RtmoPoseDetector.builder().build()) {
            List<Pose> poses = detector.detect(image);

            for (Pose pose : poses) {
                float knee = pose.angle(CocoJoint.LEFT_HIP, CocoJoint.LEFT_KNEE, CocoJoint.LEFT_ANKLE);
                System.out.printf("person %.0f%%: left knee at %.0f degrees%n",
                    pose.person().confidence() * 100, knee);
            }

            ImageAnnotator.save(ImageAnnotator.annotatePoses(image, poses), Path.of("squat-pose.png"));
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Processing
docs.text: The models are the MMPose RTMO checkpoints exported to ONNX with MMDeploy, which puts box and keypoint decoding and non-maximum suppression inside the model. The image is scaled to fit the 640 × 640 input with OpenCV's bilinear resize, placed at the top left and padded with gray, and passed as BGR with values 0–255, as for YOLOX. On seven COCO photos, inference4j returns the same people as the exported model run with OpenCV pre-processing in Python: person scores within 1e-4, boxes within 0.4 pixels, confident keypoints within 1.4 pixels.

docs.title: Drawing skeletons
docs.text:
ImageAnnotator.annotatePoses draws each pose on a copy of the image: a line for each bone of the COCO skeleton and a dot for each joint. Joints scoring below 0.3, and the bones that touch them, are not drawn.

BufferedImage annotated = ImageAnnotator.annotatePoses(image, poses);

// Custom bones, minimum joint confidence, color and line width
BufferedImage custom = ImageAnnotator.annotatePoses(image, poses, CocoJoint.edges(), 0.5f, Color.ORANGE, 3f);

Person boxes are not drawn; add them with ImageAnnotator.annotate(image, boxes) using poses.stream().map(p -> p.person().box()).toList().

docs.title: Licenses and training data
docs.text:
The wrapper code and the RTMO code and weights are Apache-2.0. For pose models, the training data matters as well: many published pose checkpoints are trained on a mix of datasets, some of which come with research-only or non-commercial terms.

The presets use the RTMO checkpoints trained on COCO only (the backbone starts from YOLOX weights, also trained on COCO). They are not the RTMO "body7" checkpoints, which add six more datasets (among them AI Challenger, CrowdPose, Halpe and MPII) and score higher.

COCO images come from Flickr under their owners' Creative Commons licenses, and the COCO annotations are CC BY 4.0. This is the same bar as the Apache-2.0 object detectors.

This page is not legal advice; check the licenses for your use.

docs.title: Bring your own weights
docs.text:
Any RTMO export with the same inputs and outputs loads through modelId and modelSource: for example a checkpoint fine-tuned on your own data, or one trained on datasets you have a commercial license for.

// A local directory with model.onnx
try (PoseDetector detector = RtmoPoseDetector.builder()
        .modelId("rtmo-s-custom")
        .modelSource(new LocalModelSource(Path.of("/models")))      // loads /models/rtmo-s-custom/model.onnx
        .build()) {
    detector.detect(Path.of("image.jpg"));
}

// Your own HuggingFace repository with model.onnx
try (PoseDetector detector = RtmoPoseDetector.builder().modelId("my-org/rtmo-m-finetuned").build()) {
    detector.detect(Path.of("image.jpg"));
}

The model must take a BGR image of shape [1, 3, size, size] with raw 0–255 values and return dets [1, N, 5] and keypoints [1, N, 17, 3], as the MMPose/MMDeploy export does. A model with a fixed input size uses that size; otherwise set it with .inputSize(int).

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text:
Method Type Description .modelId(String) String HuggingFace model ID; defaults to inference4j/rtmo-s-coco .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource Model resolution strategy; defaults to HuggingFaceModelSource .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer ONNX Runtime session config .inputSize(int) int Side of the square model input. A model with a fixed input size uses it, and a different value fails at build(); otherwise defaults to 640 .confidenceThreshold(float) float Minimum person score; defaults to 0.5. Keypoint scores never drop a person .iouThreshold(float) float IoU above which a less confident person is removed; defaults to 0.65, which the model already applies, so only a lower value changes the result .maxPoses(int) int Most poses returned per image, the most confident first; defaults to 50, the most the exported models return

The person threshold can also be set per call: detector.detect(image, 0.3f).

The exported models run non-maximum suppression themselves and return at most 50 people with a score above 0.1, so thresholds below 0.1 have no effect.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
Pose is a record with:

Member Type Description person() Detection The person's box and score, labeled person keypoints() List<Keypoint> Every joint of the model's format, in its order, whatever its score keypoint(Joint) Keypoint One joint, for example pose.keypoint(CocoJoint.LEFT_KNEE) angle(Joint a, Joint b, Joint c) float Angle at b between the lines to a and to c, in degrees (0 to 180)

Keypoint is a record with joint(), x(), y() and confidence(), and point() for a Point.

Coordinates are in the original image's pixels. A joint the model cannot see is still returned, with a low confidence and a guessed position that may lie outside the image, so check confidence() before using a joint (0.3 to 0.5 is a common cut-off).

CocoJoint is an enum of the 17 COCO joints, in the COCO order (NOSE = 0 to RIGHT_ANKLE = 16). "Left" and "right" are the person's own sides, not the viewer's. CocoJoint.edges() lists the 19 bones of the COCO skeleton. CocoJoint implements the Joint interface, so models with other keypoint formats can add their own enum later.

docs.title: Swap contract
docs.text:
Every PoseDetector follows the same contract:

  • one Pose per person, sorted by descending person confidence;
  • the person box is in pixel coordinates of the original image, inside the image, labeled person;
  • keypoints are in pixel coordinates of the original image and may fall outside it;
  • every pose has every joint of the model's format, in its order; only the person confidence filters;
  • Path and BufferedImage inputs give the same poses for the same image.

docs.title: Spring Boot
docs.text: The starter registers a PoseDetector bean when inference4j.vision.pose-detector.enabled=true; model-id and confidence-threshold are optional. See the Spring Boot guide.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Type variables as PoseDetector to keep the model swappable.
  • Check keypoint confidence before computing angles: a hidden knee gives a meaningless angle.
  • Video: decode frames yourself and pass each as a BufferedImage. The detector is thread-safe and can be shared, but it does not track people from one frame to the next.
  • Pose detection is not a safety or medical device; fall detection and similar uses need more than single-frame skeletons.

docs.title: Punctuation & Casing
docs.text:
Turn raw, unpunctuated text into readable sentences. PunctCapSegModel restores punctuation, true-cases words (including acronyms such as U.S.), and splits sentences, all in a single forward pass.

Its main use is cleaning up speech-to-text output. CTC recognizers such as Wav2Vec2 return upper-case text with no punctuation. That text is hard to read, and cased models such as NER perform poorly on it.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var model = PunctCapSegModel.builder().build()) {
    List<String> sentences = model.infer(
        "marie curie moved from poland to paris and later worked with the us radium institute "
        + "she won two nobel prizes");
    // ["Marie Curie moved from Poland to Paris and later worked with the U.S. Radium Institute.",
    //  "She won two Nobel Prizes."]
}

docs.title: With speech recognition
docs.text:
Wrap any SpeechRecognizer in PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer to get formatted transcripts directly:

try (SpeechRecognizer recognizer = new PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer(
        Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build(),
        PunctCapSegModel.builder().build())) {
    String text = recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav")).text();
    // Wav2Vec2 alone:  "MARIE CURIE MOVED TO PARIS"
    // Punctuated:      "Marie Curie moved to Paris."
}

The decorator formats only Transcription.text(). Segments pass through unchanged. Closing it closes both the wrapped recognizer and the model.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.PunctCapSegModel;
import java.util.List;

public class PunctuationExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var model = PunctCapSegModel.builder().build()) {
            List<String> sentences = model.infer("MARIE CURIE MOVED TO PARIS SHE WON TWO NOBEL PRIZES");
            sentences.forEach(System.out::println);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/punctuation-fullstop-truecase-english HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .tokenizer(UnigramTokenizer) UnigramTokenizer auto-loaded from tokenizer.json Custom tokenizer .maxLength(int) int 256 Maximum tokens per call, including the begin/end markers .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Input longer than the token limit: TRUNCATE keeps the first tokens and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Input length .stride(int) int off Process input longer than maxLength in full, as overlapping windows sharing this many tokens. When set, input is never truncated

docs.title: Result type
docs.text: infer(String) returns a List<String> with one entry per detected sentence, in order. Blank input returns an empty list.

docs.title: Input length
Available models
docs.text:
Model Wrapper Size License inference4j/punctuation-fullstop-truecase-english PunctCapSegModel ~210 MB Apache 2.0

Mirrored from 1-800-BAD-CODE/punctuation_fullstop_truecase_english. The class name mirrors PunctCapSegModelONNX from the upstream punctuators package.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The input is lower-cased, stripped of punctuation (apostrophes are kept), and whitespace-collapsed. Already-formatted text is therefore re-formatted, never double-punctuated.
  2. The text is tokenized with a SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer and wrapped in begin/end markers.
  3. A single forward pass produces three predictions per token:
    • casing: which characters of the token to upper-case
    • punctuation: none, ., ,, ?, or acronym, where a period follows every letter (us → U.S.)
    • sentence boundary: whether a sentence ends after this token
  4. The tokens are reassembled into text and split into sentences.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• English only. Supported punctuation is ., , and ?.
  • Numbers stay as the input wrote them. The model does not convert spoken numbers (FIVE FIVE FIVE) into digits.
  • A character outside the model's vocabulary appears as <unk> in the output.
  • Thread-safe: one instance can serve the whole application.

docs.title: Semantic Search
docs.text: Build a semantic search pipeline using text embeddings and cross-encoder reranking. inference4j provides two complementary models: SentenceTransformerEmbedder for fast retrieval and MiniLMSearchReranker for precision reranking.

docs.title: Quick example — embeddings
docs.text:
try (var embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/all-MiniLM-L6-v2").build()) {
    float[] embedding = embedder.encode("Hello, world!");
}

docs.title: Quick example — reranking
docs.text:
try (var reranker = MiniLMSearchReranker.builder().build()) {
    float score = reranker.score("What is Java?", "Java is a programming language.");
}

docs.title: Full search pipeline
docs.text:
A typical semantic search pipeline uses embeddings for fast candidate retrieval, then a cross-encoder reranker for precision scoring of the top results.

import io.github.inference4j.nlp.SentenceTransformerEmbedder;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.MiniLMSearchReranker;

public class SemanticSearch {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String query = "How do I handle errors in Java?";
        List<String> documents = List.of(
            "Java uses try-catch blocks for exception handling.",
            "Python decorators are a powerful feature.",
            "Error handling in Java includes checked and unchecked exceptions.",
            "The Java Stream API provides functional operations on collections."
        );

        // Stage 1: Embed and retrieve candidates by cosine similarity
        try (var embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder.builder()
                .modelId("inference4j/all-MiniLM-L6-v2").build()) {

            float[] queryEmbedding = embedder.encode(query);
            List<float[]> docEmbeddings = embedder.encodeBatch(documents);

            // Rank by cosine similarity (your own similarity function)
            // ...
        }

        // Stage 2: Rerank top candidates with cross-encoder
        try (var reranker = MiniLMSearchReranker.builder().build()) {
            float[] scores = reranker.scoreBatch(query, documents);

            for (int i = 0; i < documents.size(); i++) {
                System.out.printf("%.4f  %s%n", scores[i], documents.get(i));
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Embedder builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String — (required) HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .tokenizer(Tokenizer) Tokenizer auto-loaded WordPieceTokenizer Custom tokenizer .poolingStrategy(PoolingStrategy) PoolingStrategy MEAN Pooling method: CLS, MEAN, or MAX .normalize() — disabled Enables L2 normalization of output embeddings .textPrefix(String) String null Text prefix to prepend before encoding. encode(String, String) and encodeBatch(List, String) override it per call .maxLength(int) int 512 Maximum token sequence length .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Input longer than the token limit: TRUNCATE keeps the first tokens and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Input length .stride(int) int off Embed input longer than maxLength in full: windows sharing this many tokens (0 = consecutive chunks), averaged by the tokens each covers .dimensions(int) int off (full size) Matryoshka truncation: keep the first N values, re-normalized when .normalize() is on. Only for models trained for it (nomic-embed-text-v1.5)

docs.title: Reranker builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .tokenizer(Tokenizer) Tokenizer auto-loaded WordPieceTokenizer Custom tokenizer .maxLength(int) int 512 Maximum token sequence length .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Input longer than the token limit: TRUNCATE keeps the first tokens and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Input length .stride(int) int off Score documents longer than maxLength with MaxP: passages sharing this many tokens, each scored with the full query; the highest score wins

docs.title: Input length
Reranking long documents (MaxP)
docs.text:
With .stride(int), a document too long for one pass is split into passages, each passage is scored together with the full query, and the highest passage score is the document's score. This is the established "MaxP" technique.

try (var reranker = MiniLMSearchReranker.builder()
        .maxLength(128)
        .stride(32)
        .build()) {
    float score = reranker.score("How many people live in Berlin?", longDocument);
}

Keep passages short

ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 was trained on short MS MARCO passages, and a relevant sentence carries less weight the more unrelated text surrounds it. To measure this, we appended the sentence "Berlin has a population of about 3.7 million people…" to the end of 10 real news articles (each over 520 tokens), and scored them for the query "How many people live in Berlin?":

Setting Mean score No windowing (truncates at 512) 0.000 stride(128) with the default maxLength(512) 0.076 maxLength(256).stride(64) 0.001 maxLength(128).stride(32) 0.962 (lowest 0.872) The same articles without the sentence, MaxP 0.000

Use maxLength(128).stride(32) for MaxP. The effect also applies without MaxP: when reranking retrieved chunks, shorter chunks (around 100–150 tokens) let a relevant passage stand out. With varied text, the drop is gradual: the same sentence preceded by about 150 to 240 tokens of other text still scored 0.80–0.92 on its own.

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
encode() returns a float[] — a dense vector representation of the input text. Use cosine similarity to compare embeddings:

static double cosineSimilarity(float[] a, float[] b) {
    double dot = 0, normA = 0, normB = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        dot += a[i] * b[i];
        normA += a[i] * a[i];
        normB += b[i] * b[i];
    }
    return dot / (Math.sqrt(normA) * Math.sqrt(normB));
}

docs.title: Reranking scores
docs.text:
score() returns a float in the range [0, 1] — the sigmoid-normalized relevance score for a query-document pair. Higher means more relevant.

scoreBatch() returns a float[] — one score per document, scored against the same query.

docs.title: Pooling strategies
docs.text:
The embedder supports three pooling strategies for converting token-level representations into a single sentence embedding:

Strategy Description MEAN Average of all token embeddings (default, best for most tasks) CLS Uses only the [CLS] token embedding MAX Element-wise maximum across all token embeddings

docs.title: Available embedding models
docs.text: Model Dim Pooling Normalize Text Prefix MTEB Avg inference4j/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 384 MEAN Optional — 56.26 inference4j/all-mpnet-base-v2 768 MEAN Optional — 57.78 inference4j/bge-base-en-v1.5 768 CLS Recommended — 63.55 inference4j/gte-base 768 CLS Recommended — 61.36 inference4j/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 768 (Matryoshka: 512, 256, 128, 64) MEAN Recommended search_query: / search_document: 62.28

docs.title: BGE example
docs.text:
try (var embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/bge-base-en-v1.5")
        .poolingStrategy(PoolingStrategy.CLS)
        .normalize()
        .build()) {
    float[] embedding = embedder.encode("What is machine learning?");
}

docs.title: Nomic example (long context, prefixes, smaller vectors)
docs.text:
nomic-embed-text-v1.5 reads up to 8,192 tokens, so raise maxLength for long documents. It needs a task prefix: "search_query: " for queries and "search_document: " for documents. Pass the prefix per call, so one embedder (and one model in memory) serves both sides.

try (var embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/nomic-embed-text-v1.5")
        .maxLength(8192)
        .normalize()
        .build()) {
    float[] query = embedder.encode("What is the capital of France?", "search_query: ");
    List<float[]> documents = embedder.encodeBatch(chunks, "search_document: ");
}

A per-call prefix replaces the builder's .textPrefix(String) for that call; null means no prefix. With .stride(int), the prefix is repeated in every window.

The model was trained with Matryoshka representation learning, so .dimensions(int) can shorten its vectors with little loss. Smaller vectors cut index size and search time. Use the same dimensions for queries and documents.

Dimensions MTEB Avg 768 62.28 512 61.96 256 61.04 128 59.34 64 56.10

Scores are from the model card. The card applies a layer norm before truncating. inference4j truncates and re-normalizes without it; the two match to a cosine similarity of 0.9999 or better on our reference set.

docs.title: E5 example (with text prefix)
docs.text:
E5 models require a text prefix: "query: " for queries, "passage: " for documents.

try (var embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/e5-base-v2")
        .normalize()
        .build()) {
    float[] query = embedder.encode("What is Java?", "query: ");
    float[] passage = embedder.encode("Java is a programming language.", "passage: ");
}

If an embedder only ever sees one kind of input, set the prefix once with .textPrefix("query: ") and call encode(String).

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Two-stage pipeline: Use embeddings for fast top-K retrieval (cheap cosine similarity), then rerank the top candidates with the cross-encoder (expensive but more accurate).
  • Batch encoding: Use encodeBatch() when encoding multiple texts — more efficient than calling encode() in a loop.
  • L2 normalization: Enable .normalize() when comparing embeddings with cosine similarity. BGE, GTE, and E5 models all recommend normalization.
  • Text prefix: Some models (E5, Nomic) require a text prefix. Check the model card for the correct prefix. Use encode(text, prefix) when queries and documents need different prefixes.
  • Embedding dimension depends on the model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produces 384-dimensional vectors, while BGE/GTE/mpnet/Nomic produce 768-dimensional vectors. Nomic can be shortened with .dimensions(int).

docs.title: Sentiment Analysis
docs.text: Classify text as positive or negative (or any custom label set) using a fine-tuned DistilBERT model.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder().build()) {
    List<TextClassification> results = classifier.classify("This movie was fantastic!");
    // [TextClassification[label=POSITIVE, confidence=0.9998]]
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.DistilBertTextClassifier;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.TextClassification;
import java.util.List;

public class SentimentAnalysis {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder().build()) {
            List<String> reviews = List.of(
                "This movie was fantastic!",
                "Terrible experience, would not recommend.",
                "It was okay, nothing special."
            );

            for (String review : reviews) {
                List<TextClassification> results = classifier.classify(review);
                TextClassification top = results.get(0);
                System.out.printf("%-45s → %s (%.2f%%)%n",
                    review, top.label(), top.confidence() * 100);
            }
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .tokenizer(Tokenizer) Tokenizer auto-loaded WordPieceTokenizer Custom tokenizer .config(ModelConfig) ModelConfig auto-loaded from config.json Model config with labels .outputOperator(OutputOperator) OutputOperator auto-detected (softmax or sigmoid) Output activation .maxLength(int) int 512 Maximum token sequence length .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Input longer than the token limit: TRUNCATE keeps the first tokens and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Input length .stride(int) int off Classify long input in full, in overlapping windows sharing this many tokens. See Long texts .windowAggregation(WindowAggregation) WindowAggregation mean() How window scores combine into one score per label: mean(), max(), or your own. Requires .stride(int)

docs.title: Input length
docs.text:
Limit When exceeded Long-input strategies maxLength tokens (512 by default), including [CLS] and [SEP] Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) .stride(int): overlapping windows, whole input classified

By default only the beginning of a long text contributes to the classification.

docs.title: Long texts
docs.text:
With .stride(int) set, a text longer than maxLength tokens is split into windows that share stride tokens. Each window is classified, and a WindowAggregation combines the window scores into one score per label:

try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder()
        .stride(128)
        .windowAggregation(WindowAggregation.mean())   // the default
        .build()) {
    classifier.classify(longReview);
}
Aggregation Score per label Use it for WindowAggregation.mean() Average across windows; with softmax models still sums to 1 An overall verdict for the whole text, such as sentiment WindowAggregation.max() Highest score in any window; with softmax models no longer sums to 1 "Fires anywhere" labels, such as moderation and multi-label tagging, where one passage should decide your own lambda Anything, e.g. median or trimmed mean Custom rules

WindowAggregation is a functional interface, so a custom rule is a lambda over the list of window scores (one float[] of label probabilities per window, in text order):

WindowAggregation lastWindow = windowScores -> windowScores.get(windowScores.size() - 1);

Input that fits in one window is classified in a single pass, exactly as without stride.

docs.title: Measured accuracy
docs.text:
The default SST-2 model on 500 IMDB movie reviews longer than 512 tokens (balanced positive and negative; median 719 tokens):

Mode Accuracy Time Truncate (default) 84.8% 1× .stride(128) + mean() 87.4% 2.3× .stride(128) + max() 87.2% 2.3×

Truncated, the result matches the HuggingFace transformers pipeline on the same reviews prediction for prediction. Windowing classifies the whole review, at the cost of one model pass per window. For a two-label sentiment model, mean() and max() perform alike; max() matters for models where a single passage should decide.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
TextClassification is a record with:

Field Type Description label() String Classification label (e.g., POSITIVE) index() int Numeric class index confidence() float Confidence score (0.0 to 1.0)

docs.title: Using custom models
docs.text:
Any HuggingFace text classification model exported to ONNX will work, as long as it includes vocab.txt and config.json with id2label mappings.

try (var classifier = DistilBertTextClassifier.builder()
        .modelId("your-org/your-model")
        .build()) {
    classifier.classify("Some text");
}

The output activation (softmax vs sigmoid) is auto-detected from config.json:

  • problem_type: "multi_label_classification" → sigmoid
  • Everything else → softmax

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• The default model is fine-tuned on SST-2 (movie reviews). For other domains (product reviews, support tickets), use a model fine-tuned on relevant data.
  • Use .classify(text, topK) to limit the number of returned classifications.
  • For multi-label classification (where multiple labels can be true simultaneously), use a model with problem_type: "multi_label_classification" in its config.json.

docs.title: Speech-to-Text
docs.text:
Transcribe audio files to text. inference4j supports three speech models:

  • Moonshine (inference4j-core), Moonshine AI's English model built for live and on-device use. It generates punctuated, cased text, and spends compute only on the audio it is given.
  • Wav2Vec2 (inference4j-core), a non-autoregressive CTC model that converts speech to text in a single forward pass. Its output is upper-case and unpunctuated, so pair it with a punctuation model for readable text.
  • Whisper (inference4j-genai), OpenAI's encoder-decoder model, which generates punctuated, cased text directly and can also translate to English.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
The same 11-second recording through each option:

Option Transcript Time* Wav2Vec2 AND SO MY FELLOW AMERICANS ASK NOT WHAT YOUR COUNTRY CAN DO FOR YOU ASK WHAT YOU CAN DO FOR YOUR COUNTRY ~0.25 s Wav2Vec2 + punctuation And so my fellow Americans ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. ~0.22 s Moonshine small And so my fellow Americans, ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. ~0.26 s Moonshine tiny And so, my fellow America, ask not what your country can do for you, as what you can do for your country. ~0.14 s Whisper small And so my fellow Americans, ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. ~0.5 s

* Measured on an Apple M4 Pro CPU, with the models already loaded.

  • Moonshine: accurate, readable English with no extra dependency, and the only option that transcribes live audio while it is spoken. On long-form talks the default small model lands between whisper-tiny and whisper-small in accuracy, at an eighth of whisper-small's download (see Measured accuracy). English only.
  • Wav2Vec2: the fastest and smallest option, and part of inference4j-core with no extra dependency. Add the punctuation model when people will read the text.
  • Whisper: the most accurate and readable output, plus 99 languages and translation to English (we currently verify English transcription only). It needs the inference4j-genai module and is slower, because it generates text token by token.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var recognizer = Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build()) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("audio.wav")).text());
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.audio.Wav2Vec2Recognizer;
import io.github.inference4j.audio.Transcription;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class SpeechToText {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var recognizer = Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build()) {
            Transcription result = recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav"));
            System.out.println(result.text());
        }
    }
}

docs.title: From raw audio data
docs.text:
If you already have audio samples as a float array:

try (var recognizer = Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build()) {
    float[] audioData = loadAudioSamples(); // your audio loading logic
    Transcription result = recognizer.transcribe(audioData, 16000);
    System.out.println(result.text());
}

docs.title: Readable transcripts
docs.text:
Wav2Vec2 returns upper-case text with no punctuation, which is hard to read and a poor input for cased models such as named entity recognition. Wrap the recognizer in PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer to restore punctuation, casing and sentence boundaries:

try (SpeechRecognizer recognizer = new PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer(
        Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build(),
        PunctCapSegModel.builder().stride(64).build())) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav")).text());
}

The wrapper is itself a SpeechRecognizer, so it can be used anywhere a recognizer is expected. It formats the transcript text and each segment's text, keeping segment times; each segment costs one extra model call. Closing it closes both the recognizer and the punctuation model. stride(64) lets the punctuation model format transcripts of any length; without it, text beyond about 200 words is truncated.

The showcase app shows the difference on the same recording: the formatted transcript, with the raw Wav2Vec2 output below it for comparison.

Wav2Vec2 wrapped in PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer, compared with the raw output

See Punctuation & Casing for details and input limits.

docs.title: Whisper
docs.text:
WhisperSpeechModel lives in the inference4j-genai module and runs Whisper through onnxruntime-genai. It returns the same Transcription result:

try (var whisper = WhisperSpeechModel.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai")
        .build()) {
    System.out.println(whisper.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav")).text());
}

Two models are published: inference4j/whisper-tiny-genai (~225 MB, fastest) and inference4j/whisper-small-genai (~1.1 GB, more accurate). WhisperSpeechModel is a SpeechRecognizer, so it can replace Wav2Vec2Recognizer anywhere a recognizer is expected. It needs no punctuation wrapper, since its output is already punctuated. Whisper sees 30 seconds of audio per pass, so wrap it in SegmentedSpeechRecognizer for longer recordings. See Whisper for builder options and translation.

docs.title: Moonshine
docs.text:
MoonshineRecognizer runs Moonshine AI's Moonshine v2 models in inference4j-core. Its output is punctuated and cased, so it needs no punctuation wrapper:

try (var recognizer = MoonshineRecognizer.builder().build()) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("speech.wav")).text());
}
Model ID Parameters Download WER (Open ASR avg.)* inference4j/moonshine-streaming-tiny-en 34M 46 MB 12.00% inference4j/moonshine-streaming-small-en (default) 123M 140 MB 7.84% inference4j/moonshine-streaming-medium-en 245M 260 MB 6.65%

* Moonshine AI's figures on the Open ASR Leaderboard average, for comparison with Whisper Large v3 at 7.44%. Our own long-form measurements are under Measured accuracy.

Unlike Whisper, Moonshine has no fixed 30-second window, so a short clip costs only its own length in compute. It is still limited per call: one call transcribes at most 30 seconds (MoonshineRecognizer.MAX_SECONDS), because beyond that the model starts repeating itself. Longer audio throws IllegalArgumentException; wrap the recognizer in SegmentedSpeechRecognizer to cut it at pauses. Moonshine's own runtime ends lines after at most 15 seconds, which works well here too:

try (SpeechRecognizer recognizer = new SegmentedSpeechRecognizer(
        MoonshineRecognizer.builder().build(),
        SileroVadDetector.builder().build(),
        Duration.ofSeconds(15))) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav")).text());
}

docs.title: Live transcription
docs.text:
MoonshineRecognizer.stream(vad) transcribes continuous audio, such as a microphone, while it is being spoken. Feed audio as it arrives, in pieces of any size and at any sample rate; a voice activity detector splits it into lines at pauses, and a listener receives each line's text as it changes and once more when it is final:

try (var moonshine = MoonshineRecognizer.builder().build();
     var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder().build();
     TranscriptionStream stream = moonshine.stream(vad)
             .listener(new TranscriptListener() {
                 @Override
                 public void onLineTextChanged(TranscriptLine line) {
                     showPartial(line.text());      // may still change
                 }

                 @Override
                 public void onLineCompleted(TranscriptLine line) {
                     append(line.text());           // final
                 }
             })
             .build()) {
    while (capturing) {
        stream.addAudio(nextMicBuffer(), 48000);
    }
}   // closing completes the open line

How it works:

  1. Silero VAD scores every 32 ms of audio. A line starts when the average speech probability over the last half second rises above the detector's threshold; it includes half a second of audio from before, so the first word is not clipped.
  2. While the line is open, its audio is encoded as it arrives, and every updateInterval of audio (500 ms by default) the line is decoded again, reusing the previous text as a draft, so only the words that changed cost new work. onLineTextChanged fires when the text differs.
  3. When the speaker pauses, the line is decoded one last time and onLineCompleted fires. A completed line never changes. If the speaker never pauses, lines end at the next dip in speech after two thirds of maxLineDuration (15 seconds by default), and at the maximum at the latest.

flush() completes the open line immediately, for example when a push-to-talk button is released. Lines carry their start and end on the stream's timeline.

All work happens inside addAudio, on the calling thread, and listener events fire on that thread. Updates take tens of milliseconds, so read the microphone on one thread and pass its audio to the stream on another through a queue. One recognizer can serve several streams, each on its own thread, and they run in parallel; each open line holds its own caches. Listener events fire with no lock held: a listener may call flush() or close() on its stream, but not addAudio. Closing a stream leaves the recognizer and the detector open.

Measured by feeding the two TED-LIUM talks below in 100 ms pieces, on an Apple M4 Pro CPU limited to 4 threads:

Model Typical addAudio call Call with a text update (p50 / p95) Word error rate Moonshine tiny 0.5 ms 24 / 78 ms 6.6% Moonshine small 1 ms 51 / 147 ms 3.6%

The word error rate is slightly higher than when transcribing the whole recording with SegmentedSpeechRecognizer (5.4% and 3.3%): live lines are shorter, so the model has less context, and audio the detector scores as silence between lines is never transcribed.

Stream option Default Description .listener(TranscriptListener) does nothing Receives onLineStarted, onLineTextChanged and onLineCompleted .updateInterval(Duration) 500 ms Audio between updates of the open line's text .maxLineDuration(Duration) 15 s Longest line when the speaker does not pause; 1 to 30 s

The models are Moonshine AI's 8-bit quantized ONNX Runtime graphs, released under the MIT license. We checked our implementation against Moonshine's own runtime, token for token, on test recordings.

docs.title: Long recordings
docs.text:
SegmentedSpeechRecognizer splits long audio at pauses before passing it to any recognizer. It is essential for Whisper, which processes at most 30 seconds per pass, and also keeps memory per pass bounded for Wav2Vec2:

try (SpeechRecognizer recognizer = new SegmentedSpeechRecognizer(
        WhisperSpeechModel.builder().modelId("inference4j/whisper-small-genai").build(),
        SileroVadDetector.builder().build())) {
    System.out.println(recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav")).text());
}

How it cuts:

  1. A voice activity detector finds the speech in the recording.
  2. Each piece ends at the midpoint of the latest pause that fits within the maximum length (30 seconds by default; pass a Duration as the third constructor argument to change it).
  3. A stretch of speech with no pause at all is cut at the maximum length.
  4. The pieces' transcripts are joined with spaces.

The result carries timed segments() on the recording's timeline. When the recognizer returns its own segments, they are shifted by the piece's start time. When it returns none, as Moonshine, Wav2Vec2 and Whisper do, each non-blank piece becomes one segment that spans the piece. Pieces are cut halfway through pauses, so a segment's times include up to half a pause of silence around the speech. Audio that already fits is transcribed in one piece and gets one segment.

for (Transcription.Segment segment : recognizer.transcribe(Path.of("meeting.wav")).segments()) {
    System.out.printf("%6.1f–%6.1f s  %s%n", segment.startTime(), segment.endTime(), segment.text());
}

Closing the wrapper closes both the recognizer and the detector. It is itself a SpeechRecognizer, so it combines with PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer for Wav2Vec2.

docs.title: Measured accuracy
docs.text:
Word error rate (lower is better) Cut every 30 s SegmentedSpeechRecognizer HF transformers chunked HF transformers sequential whisper-tiny 13.2% 6.1% 6.1% 6.5% whisper-small 11.7% 3.7% 3.7% 3.9%

Measured on the 11 talks of the TED-LIUM long-form test set (148 minutes), with Whisper's standard English text normalizer. The two right-hand columns run the same models through the HuggingFace transformers reference implementation's long-form strategies (30-second chunks with 5-second overlap, and OpenAI's timestamp-driven sequential decoding). The voice activity detection adds processing time: 12% with whisper-small (302 s instead of 270 s for all 11 talks on an Apple M4 Pro CPU) and 40% with the much faster whisper-tiny (74 s instead of 53 s).

On a shorter subset of the same test set (two talks, 11.4 minutes), with SegmentedSpeechRecognizer and a 15-second maximum for every model:

Model Download Word error rate Time* whisper-small ~1.1 GB 2.4% 34 s Moonshine small 140 MB 3.3% 22 s Moonshine tiny 46 MB 5.4% 11 s whisper-tiny ~225 MB 6.0% 8 s Wav2Vec2 ~360 MB 11.7% 18 s

* All 11.4 minutes, on an Apple M4 Pro CPU limited to 4 threads per model. Over a whole recording, Moonshine tiny is slower per minute of audio than whisper-tiny, but more accurate.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text:
For MoonshineRecognizer:

Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/moonshine-streaming-small-en HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config, applied to each of the model's graphs

For Wav2Vec2Recognizer (see Whisper for WhisperSpeechModel):

Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/wav2vec2-base-960h HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .vocabulary(Vocabulary) Vocabulary auto-loaded from vocab.json CTC vocabulary .inputName(String) String auto-detected Input tensor name .sampleRate(int) int 16000 Target sample rate (Hz) .blankIndex(int) int 0 CTC blank token index .wordDelimiter(String) String "\|" Word separator token in vocabulary

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
Transcription is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The transcribed text segments() List<Segment> Timed segments. Recognizers on their own return none; SegmentedSpeechRecognizer adds one per piece

docs.title: Audio requirements
docs.text:
• Format: WAV files (loaded automatically from Path)
  • Sample rate: Audio is automatically resampled to the model's target rate (16kHz by default)
  • Channels: Mono (stereo is downmixed automatically)
  • Duration: At most 30 seconds per call for Moonshine and per pass for Whisper; use SegmentedSpeechRecognizer for longer audio. No hard limit for Wav2Vec2, but very long files use more memory.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Moonshine runs as six ONNX Runtime graphs. A frontend turns 80 ms chunks of audio into features, an encoder with sliding-window attention encodes them, an adapter turns them into the decoder's memory, and a decoder generates tokens one at a time with greedy search. The attention caches stay in ONNX Runtime memory between tokens. Decoding stops at 6.5 tokens per second of audio, which ends decodes that start repeating.

Wav2Vec2 is a non-autoregressive model — it processes the entire audio waveform in a single forward pass and produces character-level predictions using CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) decoding.

The pipeline:

  1. Load and normalize audio from WAV file
  2. Resample to 16kHz if needed
  3. Run a single forward pass through the model
  4. Apply CTC greedy decoding to convert logits to characters
  5. Join characters into words using the word delimiter

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• The default model (wav2vec2-base-960h) is trained on English LibriSpeech data. For other languages, use an appropriate fine-tuned model.
  • Wav2Vec2 output is upper-case and unpunctuated. Use PunctuatedSpeechRecognizer for readable text, or before running cased models such as NER.
  • Wav2Vec2 works best with clean speech. For noisy audio, consider preprocessing with VAD to extract speech segments first — see Voice Activity Detection.
  • Wav2Vec2 is a CTC model (single-pass), not an autoregressive model. It's fast but may be less accurate on complex audio. For better accuracy, multilingual support or translation, use Whisper.

docs.title: Text Summarization
docs.text: Summarize long articles and documents into concise text using BART or Flan-T5 encoder-decoder models.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var summarizer = BartSummarizer.distilBartCnn().build()) {
    String summary = summarizer.summarize("Long article text here...");
    System.out.println(summary);
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.BartSummarizer;

public class Summarization {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var summarizer = BartSummarizer.distilBartCnn()
                .maxNewTokens(150)
                .build()) {

            String article = """
                The Amazon rainforest, often referred to as the "lungs of the Earth",
                produces about 20% of the world's oxygen. Spanning across nine countries
                in South America, it is the largest tropical rainforest in the world,
                covering approximately 5.5 million square kilometers. The forest is home
                to an estimated 10% of all species on Earth, including over 40,000 plant
                species, 1,300 bird species, and 3,000 types of fish. Deforestation
                remains a critical threat, with an estimated 17% of the forest lost in
                the last 50 years due to logging, agriculture, and urban expansion.
                """;

            GenerationResult result = summarizer.summarize(article, token -> System.out.print(token));
            System.out.println();
            System.out.printf("%d tokens in %,d ms%n",
                    result.generatedTokens(), result.duration().toMillis());
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Using Flan-T5 as an alternative
docs.text:
FlanT5TextGenerator can also summarize text. It uses a different architecture but implements the same Summarizer interface:

import io.github.inference4j.nlp.FlanT5TextGenerator;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.Summarizer;

// Both implement Summarizer — swap freely
Summarizer summarizer = FlanT5TextGenerator.flanT5Base()
        .maxNewTokens(150)
        .build();

docs.title: BartSummarizer
docs.text: Preset Model Parameters Size BartSummarizer.distilBartCnn() DistilBART CNN 12-6 306M ~1.2 GB BartSummarizer.bartLargeCnn() BART Large CNN 406M ~1.6 GB

docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String Preset-dependent HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .tokenizerProvider(TokenizerProvider) TokenizerProvider Preset-dependent Tokenizer construction strategy .maxNewTokens(int) int 256 Maximum tokens to generate. Capped at the decoder's positions (1023 for BART, which forces a first token), with a warning; Flan-T5 has no cap .temperature(float) float 0.0 Sampling temperature (higher = more random) .topK(int) int 0 (disabled) Top-K sampling .topP(float) float 0.0 (disabled) Nucleus sampling .eosTokenId(int) int Auto-detected End-of-sequence token ID .forcedBosTokenId(int) int 0 for the BART CNN presets; otherwise forced_bos_token_id from config.json, if set Token forced as the first generated token; not part of the output text .addedToken(String) String — Register a special token for atomic encoding .maxInputLength(int) int Model limit from config.json Maximum input length in tokens .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE Longer input: TRUNCATE keeps the first tokens and logs a warning, FAIL throws InputTooLongException. See Input length

docs.title: Input length
docs.text:
Model Default limit When exceeded Long-input strategies BART / DistilBART 1024 tokens Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) MapReduceSummarizer, ChunkedSummarizer Flan-T5 512 tokens (the length T5 was trained on) Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) MapReduceSummarizer, ChunkedSummarizer

The limit comes from the model's config.json and can be changed with .maxInputLength(int).

docs.title: Long documents
docs.text:
Two decorators summarize text longer than the model's input limit. Both cut the text into chunks the model takes whole (whole sentences, up to the input limit by default) and summarize each chunk:

  • MapReduceSummarizer joins the chunk summaries and summarizes them again, repeating until they fit in one call. The result is one summary about as long as a plain call's.
  • ChunkedSummarizer returns the chunk summaries, one paragraph each. The summary grows with the text and covers all of it.
try (Summarizer summarizer = new MapReduceSummarizer(BartSummarizer.distilBartCnn().build())) {
    String summary = summarizer.summarize(longReport);
}

try (Summarizer summarizer = new ChunkedSummarizer(BartSummarizer.distilBartCnn().build())) {
    String summary = summarizer.summarize(longReport);   // one paragraph per chunk
}
  • Short input. Text that fits in one call is summarized exactly as the wrapped summarizer would.
  • Chunk size. Pass a token budget as the second constructor argument, e.g. new MapReduceSummarizer(summarizer, 512); it is capped at the model's input limit.
  • Streaming. MapReduceSummarizer streams only the final call. ChunkedSummarizer streams every chunk's summary, with the blank lines between them. In both, the streamed text equals text().
  • Result. Token counts are summed over all calls, and the duration covers the whole call.
  • Limits. Each chunk is summarized without the rest of the text. MapReduceSummarizer logs a warning if the chunk summaries stop getting shorter, and then gives them to the final call as they are.

Both work with any Summarizer that reports its token budget through summarizationLimits(); BartSummarizer and FlanT5TextGenerator do. Both are thread-safe, and closing one closes the wrapped summarizer.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
ROUGE-1 F1 (word overlap with a human summary, 0–100), with ROUGE-1 precision / recall and the average summary length:

Configuration distilbart-cnn-12-6 flan-t5-base GovReport (10 reports, 6,464 words; 583-word references) Plain: truncated at the input limit 9.8 (58 / 5, 56 words) 7.7 (70 / 5, 43 words) MapReduceSummarizer 13.3 (68 / 7, 66 words) 3.7 (62 / 2, 17 words) ChunkedSummarizer 51.4 (62 / 45, 447 words) 52.0 (60 / 48, 479 words) BillSum (15 bills, 1,920 words; 193-word references) Plain: truncated at the input limit 28.9 (58 / 21, 54 words) 15.0 (45 / 10, 35 words) MapReduceSummarizer 27.1 (56 / 20, 55 words) 15.4 (41 / 12, 35 words) ChunkedSummarizer 38.4 (42 / 44, 180 words) 33.6 (28 / 58, 420 words)
  • Where content is spread through the document (GovReport), DistilBART's map-reduce summary beats the truncated one at about the same length. Flan-T5's final call compresses the chunk summaries to a few words; use DistilBART with MapReduceSummarizer.
  • Where the key content comes first (bills open with their title, findings and purpose), truncation loses little, and map-reduce does not help.
  • ChunkedSummarizer scores highest because its longer output matches more of the long references. On GovReport its precision stays at the plain level; on BillSum it drops, as later chunks add detail the reference leaves out.

Neither model was trained on these documents (DistilBART on news, Flan-T5 on instructions), so compare rows, not absolute scores. Data: GovReport (CC-BY-4.0, Huang et al., 2021) and BillSum (CC0-1.0) test splits; greedy decoding, default maxNewTokens (256). The evaluation is LongDocumentSummarizationEvaluation in the model tests.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
Both summarize(text, tokenListener) and generate(text, tokenListener) return a GenerationResult record:

Field Type Description text() String The generated summary promptTokens() int Number of tokens in the input generatedTokens() int Number of tokens generated duration() Duration Wall-clock generation time

The convenience method summarize(text) returns the summary as a plain String.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• DistilBART CNN is purpose-built for summarization and produces the best summaries. Use it when summarization is your only task.
  • Flan-T5 is a general-purpose model that also handles translation, grammar correction, and SQL generation. Use it when you need multiple tasks from a single model.
  • Lower maxNewTokens for shorter summaries — the model will still produce coherent output.
  • Use streaming (summarize(text, token -> ...)) for long inputs where generation takes several seconds.
  • Reuse instances across calls — each one holds the model and tokenizer in memory.

docs.title: Text Detection
docs.text: Detect text regions in images using the CRAFT model. Returns bounding boxes around detected text. To also read the text, see OCR, whose default detector is PaddleOCR's line detector.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var detector = CraftTextDetector.builder().build()) {
    List<TextRegion> regions = detector.detect(Path.of("document.jpg"));
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.vision.CraftTextDetector;
import io.github.inference4j.vision.TextRegion;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class TextDetection {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var detector = CraftTextDetector.builder().build()) {
            List<TextRegion> regions = detector.detect(Path.of("document.jpg"));

            for (TextRegion r : regions) {
                System.out.printf("[%.1f, %.1f, %.1f, %.1f] (confidence=%.2f)%n",
                    r.box().x1(), r.box().y1(),
                    r.box().x2(), r.box().y2(),
                    r.confidence());
            }
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Custom thresholds
docs.text:
The defaults are those of the reference implementation (clovaai/CRAFT-pytorch). Lower textThreshold to find fainter text; raise linkThreshold if neighboring words merge into one region:

try (var detector = CraftTextDetector.builder()
        .textThreshold(0.5f)
        .linkThreshold(0.5f)
        .build()) {
    List<TextRegion> regions = detector.detect(Path.of("photo.jpg"));
}

detect(image, textThreshold, lowTextThreshold) overrides the two text thresholds for one call.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/craft-mlt-25k HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .inputName(String) String auto-detected Input tensor name .targetSize(int) int 1280 Maximum long side of the model input .magRatio(float) float 1.5 How much smaller images are scaled up, at most .textThreshold(float) float 0.7 Minimum highest text score for a region to be kept .linkThreshold(float) float 0.4 Link score above which characters are joined into words .lowTextThreshold(float) float 0.4 Text score above which a pixel belongs to a character .minComponentArea(int) int 10 Minimum region area, in score-map pixels (half the input resolution)

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
TextRegion is a record with:

Field Type Description box() BoundingBox Axis-aligned box around the region polygon() List<Point> The region's four corners, clockwise; rotated for rotated text confidence() float The region's highest text score (0.0 to 1.0)

Regions are listed by confidence, highest first.

docs.title: How CRAFT works
docs.text:
CRAFT (Character Region Awareness for Text detection) produces two score maps at half the input resolution:

  1. Text score — highlights character centers
  2. Link score — highlights the spacing between characters of a word

A pixel belongs to text where its text score exceeds lowTextThreshold or its link score exceeds linkThreshold. Each connected area whose highest text score reaches textThreshold becomes a region: its link-only pixels are removed, the rest is dilated in proportion to its thickness, and the smallest rectangle around it, rotated if the text is, gives the region's outline. Unlike YOLO-style detectors, CRAFT needs no NMS.

inference4j follows the reference implementation step by step, including its resizing (aspect ratio kept, padded to multiples of 32): on six test images (documents, a photo, a screenshot, a rotated receipt, a noisy scan) it returns the same 146 regions as the reference, with corners identical to a thousandth of a pixel.

Earlier versions

Earlier versions kept a region only if its mean text score reached textThreshold. A region's mean is around 0.55 even for clear text, so the default 0.7 found nothing, and lower thresholds kept almost everything (#130). Code that lowered the thresholds to work around this can return to the defaults.

docs.title: Hardware acceleration
docs.text:
CRAFT benefits significantly from hardware acceleration:

Backend Latency Speedup CPU 831 ms — CoreML 153 ms 5.4x 
try (var detector = CraftTextDetector.builder()
        .sessionOptions(opts -> opts.addCoreML())
        .build()) {
    detector.detect(Path.of("document.jpg"));
}

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Both Path and BufferedImage inputs are supported.
  • Images are resized keeping their aspect ratio (scaled up by at most magRatio, long side at most targetSize) and padded to multiples of 32 (VGG16 backbone requirement).
  • CRAFT detects text locations, not text content. For full OCR, use OcrPipeline; CRAFT can be its detector, which reads each word separately.
  • Coordinates are in the original image's pixel space.

docs.title: Text-to-SQL
docs.text: Generate SQL queries from natural language questions using T5-based text-to-SQL models.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var sqlGen = T5SqlGenerator.t5SmallAwesome().build()) {
    String sql = sqlGen.generateSql(
            "How many employees are in the engineering department?",
            "CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, department VARCHAR, salary INT)");
    System.out.println(sql);
    // SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees AS T1 JOIN departments AS T2
    //   ON T1.department = T2.id WHERE T2.name = 'Engineer'
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.T5SqlGenerator;

public class TextToSql {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String schema = "CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, department VARCHAR, salary INT); " +
                         "CREATE TABLE departments (id INT, name VARCHAR, location VARCHAR)";

        try (var sqlGen = T5SqlGenerator.t5SmallAwesome()
                .maxNewTokens(200)
                .build()) {

            String[] questions = {
                "What is the average salary by department?",
                "List all employees in New York",
                "Which department has the most employees?"
            };

            for (String question : questions) {
                GenerationResult result = sqlGen.generateSql(question, schema,
                        token -> System.out.print(token));
                System.out.println();
                System.out.printf("  → %d tokens in %,d ms%n",
                        result.generatedTokens(), result.duration().toMillis());
            }
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Model presets
docs.text: Preset Model Parameters Size Schema format T5SqlGenerator.t5SmallAwesome() T5-small-awesome-text-to-sql 60M ~240 MB CREATE TABLE DDL T5SqlGenerator.t5LargeSpider() T5-LM-Large-text2sql-spider 0.8B ~4.6 GB Spider format with [SEP]

docs.title: Choosing a preset
docs.text:
T5-small-awesome is recommended for most use cases. It's fast, lightweight, and handles standard SQL patterns well. Schema is provided as familiar CREATE TABLE statements.

T5-large-spider produces higher accuracy on complex queries (JOINs, subqueries, GROUP BY with HAVING). It uses a specialized schema format designed for the Spider benchmark with quoted identifiers and [SEP] table delimiters — ideal for integration with JDBC metadata.

docs.title: T5-small-awesome (CREATE TABLE DDL)
docs.text:
String schema = "CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, salary INT); "
              + "CREATE TABLE departments (id INT, name VARCHAR)";
sqlGen.generateSql("What is the average salary?", schema);

docs.title: T5-large-spider (Spider format)
docs.text:
String schema = "\"employees\" \"id\" int, \"name\" varchar, \"salary\" int, "
              + "foreign_key: primary key: \"id\" "
              + "[SEP] "
              + "\"departments\" \"id\" int, \"name\" varchar, "
              + "foreign_key: primary key: \"id\"";
sqlGen.generateSql("What is the average salary?", schema);

See Input length

docs.title: Input length
docs.text:
Model Default limit When exceeded Long-input strategies T5 presets 512 tokens (the length T5 was trained on), query and schema combined Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) None yet

Large schemas count toward the limit. Use FAIL to detect when a schema no longer fits, rather than silently losing its last tables.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
GenerationResult is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The generated SQL query promptTokens() int Number of tokens in the input generatedTokens() int Number of tokens generated duration() Duration Wall-clock generation time

The convenience method generateSql(query, schema) returns the SQL as a plain String.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use greedy decoding (default temperature=0) for SQL generation — deterministic output is what you want.
  • Always validate and sanitize generated SQL before executing it against a real database.
  • Include all relevant tables in the schema, even if the query only touches one — the model uses the full schema to resolve column references.
  • For the T5-large-spider model, the schema format can be generated programmatically from JDBC DatabaseMetaData.

docs.title: Machine Translation
docs.text: Translate text between languages using MarianMT (fixed language pairs) or Flan-T5 (flexible, any-to-any).

docs.title: Quick example
Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.generation.GenerationResult;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.MarianTranslator;

public class Translation {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var translator = MarianTranslator.builder()
                .modelId("inference4j/opus-mt-en-de")
                .maxNewTokens(200)
                .build()) {

            GenerationResult result = translator.translate(
                    "Machine learning is transforming how we build software.",
                    token -> System.out.print(token));

            System.out.println();
            System.out.printf("%d tokens in %,d ms%n",
                    result.generatedTokens(), result.duration().toMillis());
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Flexible translation with Flan-T5
docs.text:
FlanT5TextGenerator implements the Translator interface and can translate between any pair of languages using a single model:

import io.github.inference4j.nlp.FlanT5TextGenerator;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.Language;

try (var translator = FlanT5TextGenerator.flanT5Base()
        .maxNewTokens(200)
        .build()) {

    // English to French
    String french = translator.translate("Hello, how are you?",
            Language.EN, Language.FR);

    // English to German
    String german = translator.translate("Hello, how are you?",
            Language.EN, Language.DE);

    // French to Spanish
    String spanish = translator.translate("Bonjour, comment allez-vous?",
            Language.FR, Language.ES);
}

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text:
The Language enum provides constants for the most widely spoken languages. More languages will be added in future releases.

Constant Language EN English FR French DE German ES Spanish PT Portuguese PT_BR Brazilian Portuguese IT Italian NL Dutch CA Catalan SV Swedish DA Danish NO Norwegian FI Finnish PL Polish CS Czech HR Croatian RO Romanian RU Russian UK Ukrainian TR Turkish JA Japanese KO Korean AR Arabic ZH_CN Chinese Simplified ZH_TW Chinese Traditional HI Hindi

Each constant provides displayName() (e.g., "Brazilian Portuguese") and isoCode() (e.g., "pt-br").
