docs.title: Input length
docs.text:
Model Default limit When exceeded Long-input strategies MarianMT 512 tokens Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) ChunkedTranslator Flan-T5 512 tokens (the length T5 was trained on) Truncated with a warning (default), or rejected with .truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) ChunkedTranslator

The limit comes from the model's config.json and can be changed with .maxInputLength(int).

docs.title: Long documents
docs.text:
Wrap a translator in ChunkedTranslator to translate text of any length. It cuts the text into chunks the model takes whole, translates each, and joins the translations:

try (Translator translator = new ChunkedTranslator(MarianTranslator.builder()
        .modelId("inference4j/opus-mt-en-de")
        .build())) {
    String german = translator.translate(longDocument);
}
  • What a chunk holds. Whole sentences, packed up to the token budget. A chunk never spans a line break, so paragraphs, blank lines and indentation come out as they went in. A sentence too long on its own is split between words. Sentences are found with the JDK's BreakIterator.
  • Token budget. By default a chunk holds at most a quarter of the translator's maxNewTokens in input tokens (64 with the default of 256), prompt included. Short chunks fit the output limit, and models trained on sentences translate them best (see Evaluation). Set it with new ChunkedTranslator(translator, maxChunkTokens); it never exceeds the model's input limit. When a chunk's translation still reaches maxNewTokens, a warning is logged: raise maxNewTokens or lower the budget. MarianMT's decoder has 512 positions, so maxNewTokens above 512 is lowered to 512.
  • Short text that fits in one chunk is translated in one call, exactly as the wrapped translator would.
  • Streaming passes the tokens through chunk by chunk, with the whitespace between chunks; the streamed text equals text(). promptTokens() and generatedTokens() are summed over all calls, and duration() covers the whole document.
  • Limits. Each chunk is translated without the others, so context across chunks (pronouns, gender, consistent terms) can be lost at chunk boundaries.

ChunkedTranslator works with any Translator that reports its token budget through translationLimits(); MarianTranslator and FlanT5TextGenerator do. It is thread-safe, and closing it closes the wrapped translator.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
16 documents of 24 consecutive sentences each (450–550 words), with a paragraph break every four sentences, scored with chrF (character n-gram F-score, 0–100) against the full reference translation:

Configuration opus-mt-en-es flan-t5-base (en→de) Plain: whole document, truncated at 512 tokens 12.8 4.3 ChunkedTranslator, 64-token chunks 63.7 51.1 ChunkedTranslator, 128-token chunks 64.8 39.2 ChunkedTranslator, 256-token chunks 62.9 35.5 One call per sentence 65.5 56.4

Truncation is not the only loss: on the first 480 tokens of each document, which fit in one call, plain translation scored 27.1 and 10.0, while 64-token chunks scored 60.7 and 50.1. Both models were trained on short segments and drop or repeat content in long ones. Chunk runs used maxNewTokens(500).

Data: opus-mt-en-es on News Commentary en-es, which is part of the OPUS data opus-mt was trained on, so its absolute scores are inflated; flan-t5-base on WMT newstest2018 en→de. Compare rows, not columns. The evaluation is LongDocumentTranslationEvaluation in the model tests.

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
GenerationResult is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The translated text promptTokens() int Number of tokens in the input generatedTokens() int Number of tokens generated duration() Duration Wall-clock generation time

The convenience method translate(text) returns the translation as a plain String.

docs.title: Using your own MarianMT model
docs.text:
The pre-exported models under inference4j/opus-mt-* work out of the box. If you want to use a different MarianMT language pair (e.g., Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-ja), you'll need to export it yourself.

MarianTranslator expects the model directory to contain:

File Description encoder_model.onnx Encoder ONNX model decoder_model.onnx Decoder ONNX model decoder_with_past_model.onnx Decoder with KV cache config.json Model configuration tokenizer.json HuggingFace fast tokenizer format

MarianMT models require tokenizer conversion

MarianMT models on HuggingFace ship with SentencePiece files (source.spm, target.spm) and a vocab.json instead of tokenizer.json. MarianTokenizer splits text with source.spm, a SentencePiece Unigram model with its own ids, then maps each piece to the model's id through vocab.json, the vocabulary shared by source and target. A tokenizer.json converted straight from source.spm has the wrong ids, and BPE merges taken from it split words differently, so the translations are garbage or degraded.

Build a Unigram tokenizer.json whose ids come from vocab.json and whose scores come from source.spm. build_marian_tokenizer in onnx-exporter does this, and its output matches MarianTokenizer's ids:

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from optimum.exporters.onnx import main_export
from exporter.models._marian import build_marian_tokenizer

model_id = "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-ja"

# 1. Export ONNX models
main_export(
    model_name_or_path=model_id,
    output="my-model/",
    task="text2text-generation-with-past",
)

# 2. Build tokenizer.json from source.spm (segmentation) and vocab.json (ids)
build_marian_tokenizer(
    hf_hub_download(model_id, "vocab.json"),
    hf_hub_download(model_id, "source.spm"),
    "my-model/tokenizer.json",
)

MarianTranslator reads tokenizer.json as the model type it names: Unigram, or BPE for older exports.

Only standard opus-mt-* models are supported. The newer opus-mt-tc-big-* variants require target language prefixes (e.g., >>por<<) which MarianTranslator does not handle.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• MarianMT models are specialized for a single language pair (e.g., opus-mt-en-fr for English→French). They produce higher quality translations for their specific pair but require a separate model per direction.
  • Flan-T5 handles any language pair with a single model, making it more flexible but generally lower quality than a dedicated pair-specific model.
  • For bidirectional translation, you need two MarianMT models (e.g., opus-mt-en-fr and opus-mt-fr-en) — or use Flan-T5 which handles both directions.
  • Use greedy decoding (default temperature=0) for translation — sampling adds noise without improving quality.

docs.title: Visual Search
docs.text: Classify images using arbitrary text labels — no training required — powered by CLIP.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
try (ClipClassifier classifier = ClipClassifier.builder().build()) {
    List<Classification> results = classifier.classify(
            Path.of("photo.jpg"), List.of("cat", "dog", "bird", "car", "airplane"));
    System.out.println(results.get(0).label());      // "cat"
    System.out.println(results.get(0).confidence());  // 0.98
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Zero-shot classification
docs.text:
Unlike traditional image classifiers that are trained on a fixed set of labels, CLIP classifies images against any labels you provide at each call. Just pass the labels you need — no retraining, no fine-tuning, and no need to rebuild the classifier for different label sets:

try (ClipClassifier classifier = ClipClassifier.builder().build()) {
    // Emotion detection
    classifier.classify(image, List.of(
            "a photo of a happy person", "a photo of a sad person",
            "a photo of an angry person", "a photo of a surprised person"));

    // Product categorization
    classifier.classify(image, List.of(
            "a product photo of electronics", "a product photo of clothing",
            "a product photo of furniture", "a product photo of food"));

    // Scene classification
    classifier.classify(image, List.of(
            "a landscape photo of a beach", "a landscape photo of a mountain",
            "a landscape photo of a city", "a landscape photo of a forest"));
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
CLIP uses two separate encoders — one for images, one for text — trained so that matching image-text pairs produce similar embeddings. ClipClassifier wraps both encoders:

flowchart TD
    Image["Image"]
    Labels["Candidate labels<br><i>'a photo of a cat', 'a photo of a dog', ...</i>"]

    Image --> IE["ClipImageEncoder"]
    Labels --> TE["ClipTextEncoder"]

    IE --> IEmb["Image embedding<br>[512-dim]"]
    TE --> LEmb["Label embeddings<br>[512-dim] x N"]

    IEmb --> Sim["Dot-product similarity"]
    LEmb --> Sim

    Sim --> Scale["x logit scale (100)"]
    Scale --> SM["Softmax"]
    SM --> Result["List<Classification>"]

The embeddings are L2-normalized, so the dot product is a cosine similarity, which for CLIP falls in a narrow band (around 0.15 to 0.35). As in the reference implementation, the similarities are multiplied by the model's learned logit scale before the softmax (logit_scale.exp() * image_embeds @ text_embeds.T), which turns them into usable confidences. The default scale is 100, the trained value of the OpenAI CLIP checkpoints.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description modelId(String) String inference4j/clip-vit-base-patch32 HuggingFace model ID modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Where to load the model from sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer Default (CPU) ONNX Runtime session options logitScale(float) float 100 Factor applied to the cosine similarities before the softmax (the model's logit_scale.exp()). Change it only for a checkpoint trained to a different value; it affects confidences, not ranking

docs.title: Prompt tips
docs.text:
CLIP was trained on natural language captions, so passing full prompt text as labels produces better results than bare nouns. The label text is passed directly to the text encoder — format it however works best for your use case:

Use case Label examples Why General objects "a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog" Matches CLIP training data format Fine-grained "a photo of a tabby cat, a type of pet" Adds context for disambiguation Scenes "a beach landscape", "a mountain landscape" Descriptive captions Actions "a photo of a person running" Activity descriptions Styles "an impressionist style painting" Art style descriptions

docs.title: API methods
docs.text:
// Primary API — classify with candidate labels
List<Classification> classify(BufferedImage image, List<String> candidateLabels);
List<Classification> classify(BufferedImage image, List<String> candidateLabels, int topK);

// Path convenience overloads
List<Classification> classify(Path imagePath, List<String> candidateLabels);
List<Classification> classify(Path imagePath, List<String> candidateLabels, int topK);

// InferenceTask compatibility
List<Classification> run(ZeroShotInput<BufferedImage> input);

docs.title: Advanced: direct encoder access
docs.text: For use cases beyond classification — image search, image-text similarity, or custom pipelines — use ClipImageEncoder and ClipTextEncoder directly. See the CLIP Encoders reference.

docs.title: Alternative models
docs.text:
The default model is inference4j/clip-vit-base-patch32 (ViT-B/32) — the smallest and fastest variant. You can use other CLIP-compatible models by exporting them to ONNX with the same input/output layout and pointing to them via .modelId() or .modelSource(). If a checkpoint's trained logit_scale.exp() is not 100, pass it to .logitScale().

Possible variants (not yet tested with inference4j):

Model Source Embedding dim Notes openai/clip-vit-base-patch16 OpenAI 512 16×16 patches — better quality, ~2× slower openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 OpenAI 768 Best quality from OpenAI, significantly larger laion/CLIP-ViT-B-32-laion2B-s34B-b79K OpenCLIP 512 Trained on LAION-2B, often outperforms OpenAI's original laion/CLIP-ViT-L-14-laion2B-s32B-b82K OpenCLIP 768 Large variant trained on LAION-2B google/siglip-base-patch16-224 Google 768 SigLIP — improved training objective, strong zero-shot performance

Note

Models with different embedding dimensions (e.g., 768 instead of 512) will work — the wrappers don't assume a fixed size. However, you must use the same model for both image and text encoding since embeddings are only comparable within the same model's vector space.

docs.title: Model details
docs.text: Property Value Architecture ViT-B/32 (vision) + Transformer (text) Embedding dimensions 512 Image input 224×224 RGB, CLIP-normalized Text input BPE tokenized, max 77 tokens Default model inference4j/clip-vit-base-patch32 Model size ~340 MB (vision) + ~255 MB (text)

docs.title: Voice Activity Detection
docs.text: Detect speech segments in audio using Silero VAD. Returns timestamped segments with confidence scores — useful for preprocessing audio before transcription, or for detecting when someone is speaking.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder().build()) {
    List<VoiceSegment> segments = vad.detect(Path.of("meeting.wav"));
    // [VoiceSegment[start=0.50, end=3.20], VoiceSegment[start=5.10, end=8.75]]
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.audio.SileroVadDetector;
import io.github.inference4j.audio.VoiceSegment;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class VoiceActivityDetection {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder()
                .threshold(0.7f)
                .minSpeechDuration(0.3f)
                .minSilenceDuration(0.15f)
                .build()) {

            List<VoiceSegment> segments = vad.detect(Path.of("meeting.wav"));

            for (VoiceSegment seg : segments) {
                System.out.printf("%.2fs - %.2fs (duration: %.2fs, confidence: %.2f)%n",
                    seg.start(), seg.end(), seg.duration(), seg.confidence());
            }
        }
    }
}
Screenshot from showcase app

docs.title: Per-frame probabilities
docs.text:
For visualization or custom segmentation logic, extract raw speech probabilities:

try (var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder().build()) {
    float[] probabilities = vad.probabilities(Path.of("audio.wav"));
    // One probability per frame (32ms window at 16kHz)
}

docs.title: From raw audio data
docs.text:
try (var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder().build()) {
    float[] audioData = loadAudioSamples();
    List<VoiceSegment> segments = vad.detect(audioData, 16000);
}

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/silero-vad HuggingFace model ID .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .sampleRate(int) int 16000 Target sample rate (Hz) .windowSizeSamples(int) int 512 Frame window size (512 = 32ms at 16kHz) .threshold(float) float 0.5 Speech probability threshold .minSpeechDuration(float) float 0.25 Minimum speech segment duration (seconds) .minSilenceDuration(float) float 0.1 Minimum silence gap between segments (seconds) .speechPadding(float) float 0 Extends each segment by this many seconds on both sides, without overlapping neighbours

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
VoiceSegment is a record with:

Field Type Description start() float Segment start time in seconds end() float Segment end time in seconds duration() float Segment duration in seconds confidence() float Average speech probability for the segment

docs.title: Tuning thresholds
docs.text:
The default thresholds work well for clean speech. Adjust for your use case:

Scenario threshold minSpeechDuration minSilenceDuration Clean speech (default) 0.5 0.25 0.1 Noisy environment 0.7 0.3 0.15 Short utterances (commands) 0.5 0.1 0.05 Long-form speech (podcasts) 0.5 0.5 0.3

docs.title: Combining with speech-to-text
docs.text:
Use VAD to transcribe only the voiced parts of a recording. Silero's segment boundaries are tight, so audio cut exactly at a boundary can lose the first or last sound of a word. Add speechPadding when you transcribe segments:

try (var vad = SileroVadDetector.builder()
             .speechPadding(0.2f)
             .minSilenceDuration(0.3f)
             .build();
     var recognizer = Wav2Vec2Recognizer.builder().build()) {

    AudioData audio = AudioLoader.load(Path.of("meeting.wav"));
    for (VoiceSegment segment : vad.detect(audio.samples(), audio.sampleRate())) {
        int from = Math.round(segment.start() * audio.sampleRate());
        int to = Math.min(audio.samples().length, Math.round(segment.end() * audio.sampleRate()));
        String text = recognizer.transcribe(
                Arrays.copyOfRange(audio.samples(), from, to), audio.sampleRate()).text();
        System.out.printf("[%.1fs-%.1fs] %s%n", segment.start(), segment.end(), text);
    }
}
  • speechPadding(0.2f) keeps word edges inside each segment. On a short test recording, it halved the words that differed from transcribing the whole file at once (18% → 9%). Padding of 0.2–0.3 seconds worked best; at 0.5 seconds results got worse again.
  • minSilenceDuration(0.3f) stops very short pauses between words from splitting a phrase into fragments that are too short to transcribe well.
  • Padding never extends past the start or end of the audio, and neighbouring segments never overlap. When two segments are closer than twice the padding, they meet halfway.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Silero VAD is a stateful model — it maintains hidden state across frames for context. This is handled internally.
  • The model supports both 16kHz and 8kHz sample rates.
  • Use probabilities() to inspect per-frame speech likelihood for debugging or visualization.
  • For real-time applications, the 32ms window size (512 samples at 16kHz) provides low-latency detection.

docs.title: Zero-Shot Named Entity Recognition
docs.text: Extract entities of types you name at call time, such as "invoice id", "medication" or "email", with no training data and no fine-tuning. inference4j runs GLiNER, including a model tuned for personal data (PII).

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var ner = GlinerEntityRecognizer.builder().build()) {
    List<NamedEntity> entities = ner.recognize(
        "Alice Johnson paid invoice INV-2024-0042 to Acme Corp on 3 March.",
        List.of("person", "organization", "invoice id", "date"));
    // Alice Johnson (person), INV-2024-0042 (invoice id), Acme Corp (organization), 3 March (date)
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.GlinerEntityRecognizer;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.NamedEntity;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.ZeroShotEntityRecognizer;
import java.util.List;

public class PiiFinder {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String message = "Hi, I'm Alice Johnson. Reach me at alice.johnson@example.com or +1 415 555 0132. "
                + "My card is 4111 1111 1111 1111 and I live at 42 Elm Street, Springfield.";

        try (ZeroShotEntityRecognizer pii = GlinerEntityRecognizer.pii().threshold(0.3f).build()) {
            for (NamedEntity e : pii.recognize(message, List.of("person", "email", "phone number",
                    "credit card number", "address"))) {
                System.out.printf("%-20s %-28s %.2f%n", e.label(), e.text(), e.score());
            }
        }
    }
}

person               Alice Johnson                0.62
email                alice.johnson@example.com    0.98
phone number         +1 415 555 0132              0.99
credit card number   4111 1111 1111 1111          0.96
address              42 Elm Street, Springfield   0.93

docs.title: Default labels
docs.text:
recognize(String), without labels, looks for the preset's default labels, so a GLiNER recognizer also works as a NamedEntityRecognizer, in place of BertNerRecognizer. Set your own with .labels(List).

Preset Default labels small() (default) person, organization, location pii() person, email, phone number, address, date of birth, credit card number, bank account number, social security number, passport number, ip address 
try (NamedEntityRecognizer ner = GlinerEntityRecognizer.builder()
        .labels(List.of("person", "company", "product"))
        .build()) {
    ner.recognize("Marie Curie bought an Acme Rocket from Acme Corp.");
    // Marie Curie (person), Acme Rocket (product), Acme Corp (company)
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
GLiNER reads the entity types and the text together, as <<ENT>> person <<ENT>> invoice id <<SEP>> Alice Johnson paid …, and scores every span of up to 12 words against every type, all in one model run. Spans above the threshold are taken best first, and a span is dropped if it overlaps one already taken, so entities never overlap. Results come back in text order, each with the probability of its whole span.

Labels are read as plain language: "phone number" works better than "PHONE" or "tel". Results depend on the wording, so try a few on your own texts. Every type competes for the same span: offer "organization" alongside "person", or the model may file a company under "person".

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Preset Model Size Time per sentence* License small() (default) inference4j/gliner-small-v2.1, from urchade/gliner_small-v2.1 ~610 MB 9.5 ms Apache 2.0 pii() inference4j/gliner-pii-base-v1.0, from knowledgator/gliner-pii-base-v1.0 ~665 MB 10.3 ms Apache 2.0

*Laptop CPU, four ONNX Runtime threads, short news sentences.

The PII model is tuned for personal, health and payment data. Its authors suggest a threshold of 0.3.

docs.title: Accuracy on CoNLL-2003
docs.text:
On the first 1,000 sentences of the CoNLL-2003 test set (1,641 person, organization and location entities; exact span and type must match, MISC not scored), labels "person", "organization" and "location", threshold 0.5:

Model F1 Person Organization Location small() 0.683 0.892 0.452 0.626 pii() 0.681 0.870 0.503 0.619 BertNerRecognizer (distilbert-NER, trained on CoNLL-2003) 0.859 0.871 0.866 0.832

GLiNER finds people as well as a model trained on this data does. Most of its organization and location errors follow CoNLL's conventions rather than plain reading: in sports reports, CoNLL labels "Japan" or "England" a location, where GLiNER reads a team (organization). GLiNER also tags pronouns such as "he" as a person. A threshold of 0.3 lowered F1 on this data for both models. For the fixed person, organization and location types, a trained model such as BertNerRecognizer is more accurate; use GLiNER for types no trained model covers.

PII detection is not a guarantee

Detection is probabilistic: no model finds every name, number or address. Use GLiNER to reduce the personal data in text, not as the only safeguard where a missed entity matters, and check it on your own data.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/gliner-small-v2.1 HuggingFace model ID; presets small(), pii() .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .labels(List<String>) List<String> the preset's labels Entity types recognize(String) looks for .threshold(float) float 0.5 Spans scoring at or below this are ignored; in [0, 1) .multiLabel(boolean) boolean false Let the exact same span carry several labels .truncation(TruncationPolicy) TruncationPolicy TRUNCATE What to do with text over the model's word limit .stride(int) int off Read long text in full, in windows sharing this many words

docs.title: Long text
docs.text:
GLiNER counts words, not tokens: small() reads at most 384 words, pii() 2,048. By default, longer text is cut and a warning is logged once; truncation(TruncationPolicy.FAIL) throws InputTooLongException instead. With .stride(int), the whole text is read in overlapping windows of words, and each entity is taken from the window where it starts away from the edges.

try (var ner = GlinerEntityRecognizer.builder().stride(64).build()) {
    ner.recognize(longContract, List.of("person", "organization", "date", "amount"));
}

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
NamedEntity is a record with:

Field Type Description text() String The entity text, as it appears in the input label() String One of the labels passed in start() int Character offset start in the original string end() int Character offset end (exclusive) in the original string score() float Probability of the whole span (0.0 to 1.0)

docs.title: Accuracy against the gliner package
docs.text: On the same ONNX models, inference4j returns the same entities as the gliner Python package (0.2.29), with scores within 1 × 10⁻⁶, on the test texts, at thresholds 0.5 and 0.3, including text truncated at the word limit.

docs.title: Zero-Shot Text Classification
docs.text: Classify text into labels you choose at call time, with no training data and no fine-tuning: support tickets into queues, articles into topics, feedback into themes. Change the labels and the classifier follows.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
try (var classifier = DebertaZeroShotClassifier.builder().build()) {
    List<TextClassification> result = classifier.classify(
        "My invoice shows the same charge twice.",
        List.of("billing", "outage", "feature request", "account access"));
    // billing 0.97, account access 0.02, outage 0.01, feature request 0.00
}

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.DebertaZeroShotClassifier;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.TextClassification;
import io.github.inference4j.nlp.ZeroShotTextClassifier;
import java.util.List;

public class TicketRouter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> queues = List.of("billing", "outage", "feature request", "account access");

        try (ZeroShotTextClassifier classifier = DebertaZeroShotClassifier.builder()
                .hypothesisTemplate("The customer is asking about {}.")
                .build()) {
            for (String ticket : List.of(
                    "The service has been unavailable since this morning and nothing loads.",
                    "Please add a dark mode to the app.")) {
                TextClassification top = classifier.classify(ticket, queues).get(0);
                System.out.printf("%-75s -> %s (%.0f%%)%n", ticket, top.label(), top.confidence() * 100);
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The classifier is a natural language inference (NLI) model: given a text and a statement, it judges whether the text entails the statement. Each candidate label becomes a statement through the hypothesis template — "This text is about billing." — and the label's score is how strongly the text entails it. This is how HuggingFace's zero-shot-classification pipeline works, and inference4j's scores match it.

All of a text's labels are scored in one batch, so one call costs one model run per text, whatever the number of labels (up to the batch's memory).

docs.title: Single-label and multi-label
Writing labels and templates
docs.text:
• Labels are read as plain language. "feature request" works better than "FR" or "feat_req".
  • The template matters. The default, "This text is about {}.", suits topics. A template written for your texts, such as "The customer is asking about {}." or "The sentiment of this review is {}.", often scores better. {} stands for the label.
  • Validate on your own data. Zero-shot accuracy varies a lot between tasks. Try a few templates and label wordings on a sample of labeled texts before relying on it.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Preset Model Size AG News accuracy* Time per text* base() (default) inference4j/deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0-c ~740 MB 64.0% 47 ms large() inference4j/deberta-v3-large-zeroshot-v2.0-c ~1.7 GB 78.7% 150 ms

*400 texts from the AG News test split, four topics (World, Sports, Business, Science and Technology), default template, single-label; laptop CPU, four ONNX Runtime threads. On the author's broader benchmark of 28 classification tasks, the models reach a mean F1 of 0.619 (base) and 0.676 (large), against 0.497 for facebook/bart-large-mnli.

Both are Moritz Laurer's zero-shot v2.0 "-c" models: MIT-licensed and trained only on commercially-friendly data (synthetic data plus the MNLI and FEVER-NLI datasets).

docs.title: Other NLI models
docs.text:
.modelId(String) accepts other NLI models exported to ONNX with a Unigram tokenizer.json. The classes are read from id2label in config.json:

  • the entailment class is the label starting with "entail", and is required;
  • the class it is scored against in multi-label mode, or with a single label, is the label starting with "contradict". A model without one, such as {0: entailment, 1: not_entailment}, uses the other class: the last class when entailment is first, otherwise the first.

The order of the classes does not matter: {0: entailment, 1: contradiction, 2: neutral} and {0: contradiction, 1: neutral, 2: entailment} both score entailment against contradiction.

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text: Method Type Default Description .modelId(String) String inference4j/deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0-c HuggingFace model ID; presets base(), large() .modelSource(ModelSource) ModelSource HuggingFaceModelSource Model resolution strategy .sessionOptions(SessionConfigurer) SessionConfigurer default ONNX Runtime session config .hypothesisTemplate(String) String "This text is about {}." How a label becomes a hypothesis; {} is the label .multiLabel(boolean) boolean false Score labels independently instead of letting them compete .maxLength(int) int 512 Maximum tokens per model run, text, hypothesis and special tokens included .stride(int) int off Score long text in full, in windows sharing this many tokens .windowAggregation(WindowAggregation) WindowAggregation mean() single-label, max() multi-label How window scores combine. Requires .stride(int)

docs.title: Long text
docs.text:
By default, text that does not fit in maxLength tokens together with a hypothesis is cut at its end; the hypothesis is always kept whole, as in HuggingFace. With .stride(int), the whole text is scored in overlapping windows and the window scores combined: by default mean() for single-label (an overall verdict) and max() for multi-label (a label that applies anywhere in the text applies to the text).

try (var classifier = DebertaZeroShotClassifier.builder().stride(128).build()) {
    classifier.classify(longReport, List.of("finance", "legal", "engineering"));
}

docs.title: Result type
docs.text:
TextClassification is a record with:

Field Type Description label() String The candidate label index() int The label's position in the list passed in confidence() float The label's score (0.0 to 1.0)

Results are sorted by confidence, highest first.

docs.title: Accuracy against HuggingFace
docs.text: On the same ONNX model, inference4j's scores equal those of HuggingFace's tokenizer and post-processing to within 4 × 10⁻⁷. Compared with the zero-shot-classification pipeline running the original PyTorch weights, scores differ by up to 3 × 10⁻⁴ (more on texts near 512 tokens), the ordinary difference between ONNX and PyTorch arithmetic; the top label agreed on all 400 AG News texts and all test cases, and accuracy was identical.
